Claude Code 2.1.101 Deep Dive: New Team Collaboration Tools & Enterprise Deployment Improvements

Apr 11, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Claude Code 2.1.101 Deep Dive Report

Section titled “Claude Code 2.1.101 Deep Dive Report”

Release: April 2026 (extracted from CHANGELOG.md) Previous version: 2.1.98 | Analysis generated: 2026-04-11

Overview

Section titled “Overview”

2.1.101 is a medium-sized update containing 2 new features, 13 improvements, and 25+ fixes. Core themes:

  1. New team collaboration tools — /team-onboarding command for one-click team onboarding guide generation
  2. Zero-config enterprise infrastructure — OS CA certificate store trusted by default, TLS proxies work out of the box
  3. Lower barriers to cloud features — /ultraplan and other remote features auto-create default cloud environments
  4. Continued stability polish — Numerous fixes for --resume, permissions, plugins, and rendering issues

1. New Features in Detail

Section titled “1. New Features in Detail”

1.1 /team-onboarding — Team Onboarding Guide Generator

Section titled “1.1 /team-onboarding — Team Onboarding Guide Generator”

What changed: New /team-onboarding command that automatically generates a quick-start guide for team members based on your local Claude Code usage patterns.

Background: After adopting Claude Code, each experienced user accumulates their own best practices — custom slash commands, common MCP server configurations, permission rules, workflow habits, etc. When new members join, there’s no structured onboarding material; knowledge spreads only by word of mouth.

Use cases:

  • Tech leads generating project-specific Claude Code guides for new engineers
  • Teams standardizing Claude Code configurations to ensure consistent toolchains
  • Open source maintainers providing AI-assisted development onboarding docs for contributors

Technical details:

  • Likely analyzes local settings.json, CLAUDE.md, installed plugins, MCP configurations, etc.
  • Outputs a structured document with recommended settings, common commands, and project-specific tips

Comparison with alternatives:

  • Codex CLI: No similar feature; team onboarding is entirely manual
  • Cursor: Has shareable .cursorrules, but no auto-generated onboarding docs
  • This feature reflects Claude Code’s continued investment in team collaboration

1.2 OS CA Certificate Store Trusted by Default

Section titled “1.2 OS CA Certificate Store Trusted by Default”

What changed: The OS CA certificate store is now trusted by default, so enterprise TLS proxies work without extra configuration. Set CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE=bundled to fall back to bundled CAs only.

Background: Enterprise environments commonly use TLS MITM proxies (Zscaler, Netskope, Palo Alto, etc.) for traffic inspection. These proxies use enterprise self-signed CA certificates, and Node.js doesn’t trust the OS certificate store by default, causing frequent UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE errors in corporate networks.

Use cases:

  • Enterprise users no longer need to set the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS environment variable
  • IT admins have one fewer configuration step when deploying Claude Code
  • Works out of the box behind various enterprise security gateways

Notes:

  • If you encounter certificate compatibility issues, fall back with CLAUDE_CODE_CERT_STORE=bundled
  • This change is transparent to non-enterprise users

Historical context: 2.1.94 fixed Bedrock SigV4 auth Bearer Token issues, and 2.1.98 fixed Bedrock 403 errors with empty string environment variables. Certificate trust is another important fix for enterprise deployment pain points.

1.3 /ultraplan Auto-Creates Default Cloud Environments

Section titled “1.3 /ultraplan Auto-Creates Default Cloud Environments”

What changed: /ultraplan and other remote session features now automatically create a default cloud environment without requiring prior setup in the web UI.

Background: Previously, using /ultraplan required first visiting the claude.ai web UI to create a cloud environment — a prerequisite that often confused users: “I’m working fine in the terminal, why do I need to open a browser?”

Use cases:

  • Start using /ultraplan immediately on first use without interrupting your workflow
  • Lower the barrier to remote features, letting more users experience cloud capabilities

2. Key Improvements

Section titled “2. Key Improvements”

2.1 Brief Mode Enhancement

Section titled “2.1 Brief Mode Enhancement”

Claude now automatically retries once when it responds with plain text (instead of structured messages) in brief mode. This reduces occasional formatting anomalies in brief mode.

2.2 Focus Mode Improvement

Section titled “2.2 Focus Mode Improvement”

Claude now knows that users can only see the final message in focus mode, so it writes more self-contained summaries. Previously, context from intermediate steps could be lost, resulting in summaries missing key information.

2.3 Significantly Better Error Messages

Section titled “2.3 Significantly Better Error Messages”

This update substantially improves several categories of error messages:

  • Tool unavailable errors: Now explain why and guide users on how to handle it, instead of a bare error
  • Rate limit retries: Show which specific limit was hit and when it resets, replacing opaque countdown timers
  • Refusal errors: Include the specific explanation provided by the API

These improvements significantly affect daily experience, especially during heavy usage near rate limits.

2.4 --resume Supports Session Titles

Section titled “2.4 --resume Supports Session Titles”

claude -p --resume <name> now accepts session titles set via /rename or --name, no longer limited to session IDs. This is SDK and automation friendly.

2.5 Settings Fault Tolerance

Section titled “2.5 Settings Fault Tolerance”

Unrecognized hook event names in settings.json no longer cause the entire file to be ignored. Previously, a single typo could disable all configuration — this fix greatly improves config robustness.

2.6 OTEL Tracing Privacy Controls

Section titled “2.6 OTEL Tracing Privacy Controls”

Beta tracing now respects OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS, OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS, and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_CONTENT flags. Sensitive span attributes are no longer sent by default and require explicit opt-in. This is important for enterprise compliance.

2.7 SDK query() Resource Cleanup

Section titled “2.7 SDK query() Resource Cleanup”

The SDK’s query() method now properly cleans up subprocesses and temporary files when consumers break or use await using. Previously, this could lead to zombie processes and /tmp directory bloat.

3. Security Fixes

Section titled “3. Security Fixes”

3.1 LSP Command Injection Vulnerability (High Severity)

Section titled “3.1 LSP Command Injection Vulnerability (High Severity)”

Fix: Patched a command injection vulnerability in LSP binary detection via the POSIX which fallback path.

Risk assessment: This is an exploitable security vulnerability. Attackers could potentially execute arbitrary commands through a crafted LSP server path. All users should upgrade as soon as possible.

3.2 Permission System Fixes

Section titled “3.2 Permission System Fixes”
  • permissions.deny rules now correctly override PreToolUse hook’s permissionDecision: "ask" — previously hooks could downgrade deny to prompt
  • Fixed an issue where background cleanup ignored cleanupPeriodDays and deleted session history older than 30 days when --setting-sources didn’t include user

4. Notable Bug Fixes

Section titled “4. Notable Bug Fixes”

4.1 --resume Fixes (4 items)

Section titled “4.1 --resume Fixes (4 items)”

The --resume feature received extensive fixes in this release, continuing a trend across multiple recent versions:

  • Loader anchored to dead branches instead of the active conversation in large sessions, causing context loss
  • Chain resume crossed over into unrelated subagent conversations
  • Persisted Edit/Write tool results missing file_path caused crashes
  • Multiple UI issues with the /resume picker (narrow viewport, unreachable Windows Terminal preview, incorrect workspace cwd, etc.)

4.2 Timeout & Backend Compatibility

Section titled “4.2 Timeout & Backend Compatibility”

Fixed a hardcoded 5-minute request timeout that previously ignored API_TIMEOUT_MS settings and interrupted slow backends (local LLMs, extended thinking, slow gateways). This is especially important for users running local models or self-hosted deployments.

4.3 Subagent Fixes (3 items)

Section titled “4.3 Subagent Fixes (3 items)”
  • Subagents didn’t inherit dynamically injected MCP server tools
  • Subagents in isolated worktrees were denied read/write access to files within their own worktree
  • Bedrock SigV4 auth failed when an Authorization header was set

4.4 Plugin System Fixes (5 items)

Section titled “4.4 Plugin System Fixes (5 items)”
  • Slash commands conflicting with plugin parsing due to duplicate name: frontmatter
  • /plugin update failing with ENAMETOOLONG
  • Discover showing already-installed plugins
  • Directory-source plugins loading from stale cache
  • Skills not respecting context: fork and agent frontmatter fields

4.5 Rendering & UI Fixes

Section titled “4.5 Rendering & UI Fixes”
  • Flickering on content changes in non-fullscreen mode
  • Terminal scroll buffer being cleared in long sessions
  • Mouse scroll escape sequences leaking into prompt input
  • ctrl+], ctrl+\, ctrl+^ not triggering in terminals that send raw C0 control bytes
  • /login OAuth URL rendered with extra padding

4.6 Other Important Fixes

Section titled “4.6 Other Important Fixes”
  • Crash when environment variable values in settings.json are numbers instead of strings
  • Custom key bindings not loading on Bedrock, Vertex, and other third-party providers
  • claude --continue -p not correctly continuing sessions created by -p or SDK
  • Grep tool ENOENT when embedded ripgrep path is stale (VS Code extension auto-updates, macOS App Translocation)
  • /btw writing a full conversation copy on every use
  • Multiple Remote Control issues fixed

5. Version Jump Explanation

Section titled “5. Version Jump Explanation”

The version jumps from 2.1.98 directly to 2.1.101, skipping 2.1.99 and 2.1.100. This occasionally happens in Claude Code’s version history, typically because intermediate versions had issues discovered during internal testing and weren’t released publicly, or version numbers were allocated to hotfix branches.

6. Upgrade Recommendations

Section titled “6. Upgrade Recommendations”

Must Upgrade ⚠️

Section titled “Must Upgrade ⚠️”
  • The LSP command injection vulnerability is the most critical security fix — all users should upgrade ASAP
  • Users of the --resume feature will see significant stability improvements

Recommended Upgrade 👍

Section titled “Recommended Upgrade 👍”
  • Enterprise users will benefit from CA certificate trust and OTEL privacy controls
  • Users with local LLMs or slow backends are no longer constrained by the 5-minute hard timeout
  • Heavy plugin users will benefit from multiple fixes

Optional Upgrade

Section titled “Optional Upgrade”
  • /team-onboarding is valuable for team leads but not urgent
  • Brief mode and Focus mode improvements are quality-of-life enhancements

7. Trend Observations

Section titled “7. Trend Observations”
  1. --resume is the biggest ongoing stability challenge: 5+ consecutive versions have included numerous /resume-related fixes, indicating the extreme complexity of session persistence and recovery
  2. Enterprise deployment barriers keep falling: From Bedrock wizard (2.1.92) → Vertex AI wizard (2.1.98) → CA certificate trust (2.1.101), enterprise-friendliness improves steadily
  3. Plugin ecosystem is maturing but still fragile: Every version includes plugin-related fixes, indicating the plugin system is still iterating rapidly
  4. Team features are emerging: /team-onboarding is the first explicitly team-collaboration-oriented feature, signaling Claude Code’s evolution from a personal tool to a team tool

OpenClaw 2026.4.10 Changelog Deep Dive: Native Codex Integration, Active Memory & Local MLX Voice

Apr 11, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Overview

Section titled “Overview”

2026.4.10 is a heavyweight release, shipped on April 11, 2026. It contains 17 new features and 20+ fixes, covering model integration, memory systems, voice, security hardening, and multi-channel fixes.

Three highlights:

  1. Native Codex Integration — OpenAI Codex as a built-in provider, independent from the OpenAI channel
  2. Active Memory Plugin — Automatic memory recall without manual user triggers
  3. Local MLX Voice — macOS Talk Mode supports local MLX voice inference

New Features

Section titled “New Features”

1. Models/Codex — Native Codex Provider

Section titled “1. Models/Codex — Native Codex Provider”
  • What changed: Added built-in Codex provider and plugin-level app-server harness. codex/gpt-* models use Codex-specific authentication, threads, model discovery, and compaction paths. openai/gpt-* retains the original OpenAI provider path.
  • Background: Previously, Codex models reused the OpenAI provider path, unable to leverage Codex’s native OAuth authentication, session thread management, and context compaction capabilities. Mixing two model sets in one provider caused authentication and feature conflicts.
  • Use cases: When configuring codex/gpt-4.1 or codex/gpt-5 as the model, it automatically uses the Codex authentication flow (OAuth) with native threading and compaction. Ideal for long coding sessions.
  • Notes: Requires configuring Codex OAuth scopes; existing openai/gpt-* configurations are unaffected; first use after upgrade requires completing OAuth authorization.
  • Evolution: OpenClaw initially supported only a single OpenAI provider → later added multi-provider architecture (OpenRouter, Anthropic, Ollama, etc.) → this version elevates Codex to a first-class independent provider.
  • Competitive landscape: Most similar products still treat Codex as an OpenAI variant without independent provider separation.
  • Future trends: Subsequent versions are expected to establish independent provider paths for more OpenAI sub-products (e.g., Sora, DALL·E).

2. Memory/Active Memory — Automatic Memory Recall Plugin

Section titled “2. Memory/Active Memory — Automatic Memory Recall Plugin”
  • What changed: Added optional Active Memory plugin that automatically runs a memory sub-agent before the main reply, pulling relevant preferences, context, and historical details. Supports message/recent/full context modes, /verbose real-time inspection, advanced prompt/thinking overrides, and optional transcript persistence.
  • Background: Previously, users had to manually say “remember this” or “search memory” to trigger the memory system. Useful context in daily conversations was being missed, rendering the memory system largely ineffective.
  • Use cases: When a user mentions “I’m going to Tokyo next week” in casual conversation, Active Memory automatically records and recalls it in subsequent conversations. No explicit commands needed. Configuration example: enable the plugin with context: "recent" mode, and the agent automatically queries recent relevant memories before each reply.
  • Notes: Adds latency to each reply (extra sub-agent call); increased token consumption; recommend starting with message mode (lightest) to evaluate before upgrading to full mode. Use /verbose to observe the recall process.
  • Evolution: OpenClaw memory system evolution: manual memory_search → MEMORY.md files → Dreaming (sleep-time memory consolidation) → this version’s Active Memory (real-time auto-recall).
  • Future trends: Active Memory + Dreaming will form a complete “remember-consolidate-recall” loop, with subsequent versions expected to optimize their synergy.

3. macOS/Talk — Local MLX Voice Provider

Section titled “3. macOS/Talk — Local MLX Voice Provider”
  • What changed: Added experimental local MLX voice provider supporting explicit provider selection, local audio playback, interruption handling, and system voice fallback.
  • Background: Talk Mode previously relied on cloud TTS services (e.g., ElevenLabs), suffering from high latency, privacy concerns, and network dependency. Apple Silicon chips on macOS are fully capable of running voice models locally.
  • Use cases: Using Talk Mode offline; privacy-sensitive conversation scenarios; automatic fallback to system voice when network is unstable.
  • Notes: macOS Apple Silicon (M1+) only; experimental feature — voice quality may not match cloud services; requires downloading MLX voice models.
  • Evolution: Talk Mode: cloud TTS only → this version adds local MLX option, evolving toward a hybrid architecture.

4. Tools/Video Generation — Seedance 2.0 Support

Section titled “4. Tools/Video Generation — Seedance 2.0 Support”
  • What changed: Added Seedance 2.0 model reference for the built-in fal provider, submitting duration, resolution, audio, seed and other provider-specific fields.
  • Use cases: Generate videos through OpenClaw using fal’s Seedance 2.0, with control over duration, resolution, audio, and other parameters.
  • Notes: Requires fal API key; video generation is asynchronous and time-consuming.

5. Microsoft Teams — Enhanced Message Actions

Section titled “5. Microsoft Teams — Enhanced Message Actions”
  • What changed: Added pin, unpin, read, react, and list reactions message actions.
  • Use cases: Agents can pin important messages, add emoji reactions, and mark as read.

6. QA/Matrix — Matrix Live Test Channel

Section titled “6. QA/Matrix — Matrix Live Test Channel”
  • What changed: Added live QA test channel based on disposable Matrix homeservers, covering threads, reactions, restarts, and allowlist behavior.
  • Use cases: Automated Matrix channel integration tests in CI/CD pipelines.

7. QA/Telegram — Telegram Live Test Channel

Section titled “7. QA/Telegram — Telegram Live Test Channel”
  • What changed: Added Telegram private group bot-to-bot test channel, hardened artifact handling, maintaining native Telegram command reply threads.

8. QA/Multipass — Virtual Machine Test Runner

Section titled “8. QA/Multipass — Virtual Machine Test Runner”
  • What changed: Added --runner multipass option allowing QA scenarios to run in disposable Linux VMs.

9. CLI/exec-policy — Execution Policy Management Command

Section titled “9. CLI/exec-policy — Execution Policy Management Command”
  • What changed: Added openclaw exec-policy command with show/preset/set subcommands for syncing tools.exec.* configuration with local exec approval files.
  • Use cases: openclaw exec-policy show to view current policy; openclaw exec-policy preset strict to quickly switch to strict mode.

10. Gateway/commands.list RPC

Section titled “10. Gateway/commands.list RPC”
  • What changed: Added commands.list RPC allowing remote gateway clients to discover runtime native commands, text commands, skill commands, and plugin commands.

11. Models/providers — Private Network Endpoint Support

Section titled “11. Models/providers — Private Network Endpoint Support”
  • What changed: Added models.providers.*.request.allowPrivateNetwork configuration allowing trusted self-hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
  • Use cases: Connect to intranet-deployed vLLM, Ollama, and other OpenAI-compatible services.
  • Notes: Limited to model request surface only; does not affect other security policies. Must be enabled per provider.

12. Feishu — AI Agent Registration

Section titled “12. Feishu — AI Agent Registration”
  • What changed: Standardized request User-Agent, registering the bot as an AI Agent.

13. Matrix/Partial Streaming — MSC4357 Live Markers

Section titled “13. Matrix/Partial Streaming — MSC4357 Live Markers”
  • What changed: Added MSC4357 live markers for draft previews, supporting client-side typewriter animation rendering.

14. Control UI/Dreaming — Scene and Diary UI Improvements

Section titled “14. Control UI/Dreaming — Scene and Diary UI Improvements”
  • What changed: Simplified Scene and Diary interfaces, stabilized pending entry sorting.

15. Agents — GPT-5 Strict Execution Contract

Section titled “15. Agents — GPT-5 Strict Execution Contract”
  • What changed: Added optional strict-agentic embedded Pi execution contract where plan-only or filler turns continue executing until hitting a genuine blocker.
  • Use cases: Enable when using GPT-5 series models to ensure the agent keeps working until truly complete or blocked.
  • Notes: Opt-in feature requiring explicit enablement; may increase token consumption.

16. Agents/OpenAI — Codex Tool Compatibility

Section titled “16. Agents/OpenAI — Codex Tool Compatibility”
  • What changed: Added OpenAI/Codex tool schema compatibility and embedded run replay/liveness state.

17. Docs i18n — Documentation Translation Improvements

Section titled “17. Docs i18n — Documentation Translation Improvements”
  • What changed: Chunked translation of source documents, rejection of truncated tag output, recovery from terminated translation sessions.

Fixes

Section titled “Fixes”

1. Browser/Security — Browser Security Hardening (Major)

Section titled “1. Browser/Security — Browser Security Hardening (Major)”
  • What changed: Comprehensive hardening of browser and sandbox navigation defenses: strict SSRF defaults, hostname whitelist, interaction-driven redirects, subframes, CDP discovery, existing sessions, tab operations, noVNC, marker-span sanitization, Docker CDP origin scope enforcement.
  • Notes: ⚠️ May affect existing browser automation scripts after upgrade, especially those accessing intranet addresses.

2. Security/Tools — Tool Security Hardening (Major)

Section titled “2. Security/Tools — Tool Security Hardening (Major)”
  • What changed: Hardened exec preflight reads, host environment variable blocklist, node output boundaries, third-party media reads, profile change authorization, plugin install dependency scanning, tool hooks, token sanitization, oversized WebSocket frame handling.
  • Notes: ⚠️ Multiple security hardening measures may affect existing workflows. Full regression testing recommended.

3. OpenAI/Codex — Codex Integration Fixes

Section titled “3. OpenAI/Codex — Codex Integration Fixes”
  • What changed: Added required Codex OAuth scopes, improved provider/runtime error classification, stopped suggesting /elevated full when host exec is unavailable, maintained embedded run replay/liveness state.

4. CLI/WhatsApp Media Send Fix

Section titled “4. CLI/WhatsApp Media Send Fix”
  • What changed: Gateway mode --media sends now use the channel sendMedia path, fixing silent file drops when sending WhatsApp documents and attachments.

5. Microsoft Teams — Major Fixes

Section titled “5. Microsoft Teams — Major Fixes”
  • What changed: Fixed personal DM media download, Bot Framework conversations, OneDrive/SharePoint shared files, conversation IDs, Bot Framework audience tokens, SSO login callbacks, thread reply context injection, cron announcement delivery.
  • Notes: Teams users are strongly recommended to upgrade.

6. Gateway/Tailscale — Startup Order Optimization

Section titled “6. Gateway/Tailscale — Startup Order Optimization”
  • What changed: Tailscale exposure and update checks now execute before channel/plugin sidecar startup.

7. Gateway/Startup — Startup Stability

Section titled “7. Gateway/Startup — Startup Stability”
  • What changed: WebSocket RPC remains available during channel/plugin startup; chat.history delayed until sidecar completion; refreshed gateway methods after delayed plugin reload; upgrade flood protection.

8. WhatsApp — Reconnection Stability

Section titled “8. WhatsApp — Reconnection Stability”
  • What changed: Preserved inbound replies, media, composing indicators, and queued outbound delivery across reconnection gaps.

9. Gateway/Thread Routing — Thread Routing Fixes

Section titled “9. Gateway/Thread Routing — Thread Routing Fixes”
  • What changed: Maintained delivery targets for Slack, Telegram, Mattermost, Matrix, and agent announcements.

10. Models/Fallback — Model Fallback Stability

Section titled “10. Models/Fallback — Model Fallback Stability”
  • What changed: Maintained /models selection across transient failures and config reloads; supported timeout cooldown probes; detected context overflow.

11. Agents/BTW — Side-question Feature Fix

Section titled “11. Agents/BTW — Side-question Feature Fix”
  • What changed: Fixed /btw failure after tool-use turns, cleaned up replayed tool blocks, hidden reasoning, and malformed image payloads.

12. Commands/Targeting — Multi-Agent Command Targeting Fix

Section titled “12. Commands/Targeting — Multi-Agent Command Targeting Fix”
  • What changed: Command output, send strategy, usage/cost, context reports, and model lists now use the selected agent/session rather than the requester.

13. iMessage/Self-Chat — Self-Chat Distinction

Section titled “13. iMessage/Self-Chat — Self-Chat Distinction”
  • What changed: Distinguished regular DMs from true self-chat using destination ID + chat participants.

14. Agents/Timeouts — Timeout Optimization

Section titled “14. Agents/Timeouts — Timeout Optimization”
  • What changed: Default LLM idle window extended to 120s; recovery paths maintain quiet timeouts.
  • Notes: Default timeout extended to 120s; check custom configurations.

15. Gateway/Agents — Agent Configuration Preservation

Section titled “15. Gateway/Agents — Agent Configuration Preservation”
  • What changed: Preserved model selection and IDENTITY.md content during agent create/update and workspace moves.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Upgrade Recommendations

Section titled “Upgrade Recommendations”
  1. Strongly recommended to upgrade — this version contains numerous security fixes (browser SSRF, tool security); delaying upgrade poses security risks
  2. Considerations:
    • Browser security hardening may affect existing automation scripts
    • Exec preflight and environment variable blocklist may affect some exec workflows
    • Default LLM timeout extended to 120s — check custom configurations
    • Codex integration requires completing OAuth authorization
  3. Upgrade order: Test on non-critical instances first, then roll out to production
  4. Special attention: WhatsApp users, Teams users, and Tailscale remote management scenarios all have important fixes

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”
  1. Memory systems moving toward full automation — Active Memory + Dreaming combination trends toward a complete memory loop
  2. Local inference continues to strengthen — MLX voice is the beginning, likely expanding to local model inference
  3. Security defense in depth — Each version hardens security boundaries, trending toward zero-trust architecture
  4. QA infrastructure professionalization — Matrix, Telegram, Multipass VM test channels indicate OpenClaw is building enterprise-grade QA infrastructure
  5. Multi-provider ecosystem — Independent Codex, allowPrivateNetwork, etc. are paving the way for a richer model ecosystem

Vibe Sparking

Setting up claude-cli/claude-opus-4-6 as an optional model in OpenClaw, calling the Anthropic API through the local Claude Code CLI’s OAuth authentication. What seemed like a simple one-step operation turned into two major debugging sessions.

Configuration Steps

Section titled “Configuration Steps”

1. Adding the Auth Profile

Section titled “1. Adding the Auth Profile”

Register Claude CLI’s OAuth credentials (without setting it as default):

This command will:

  • Read OAuth credentials from the Claude CLI keychain
  • Create a claude-cli provider in openclaw.json
  • Add an auth profile in auth-profiles.json (type: oauth)

Note: No --set-default flag — this is meant as a fallback model only.

2. Cleaning Up Extra Models

Section titled “2. Cleaning Up Extra Models”

The command adds multiple models by default (sonnet, opus-4-5, haiku, etc.). Keep only what you need:

3. Fixing the asdf Shim Conflict (The Big One)

Section titled “3. Fixing the asdf Shim Conflict (The Big One)”

Symptom: Selecting claude-cli/claude-opus-4-6 silently falls back to another model.

Log error:

Root cause: Two Claude CLI installations coexisting:

  • ~/.asdf/installs/nodejs/22.11.0/bin/claude — old version (installed via npm global)
  • ~/.local/bin/claude — new version (official standalone install)

The Gateway process resolves claude through asdf’s shim, but the working directory’s .tool-versions doesn’t specify the matching Node.js version, causing asdf to intercept and fail.

Fix: Remove the old Claude CLI from asdf so the shim stops intercepting:

After the fix, Gateway correctly finds ~/.local/bin/claude.

4. Hitting the Billing Wall

Section titled “4. Hitting the Billing Wall”

With the asdf issue resolved, a new 402 error appeared:

Anthropic has separated third-party app usage (like Claude Code CLI) from subscription plan limits. You need to claim credits at claude.ai/settings/usage before the model will work.

Final Configuration

Section titled “Final Configuration”

Model Config

Section titled “Model Config”

Auth Profile

Section titled “Auth Profile”

Current Limitations

Section titled “Current Limitations”
LimitationDetails
Billing credits not activatedMust claim at claude.ai/settings/usage
OAuth token expiryTokens expire and need periodic refresh
Depends on local Claude CLIRequires ~/.local/bin/claude to be executable and logged in
Lowest fallback priorityLast in the fallback chain, used only when all others fail
200k context windowCompared to the billing proxy’s 1M context, claude-cli is limited to 200k

Takeaway

Section titled “Takeaway”

claude-cli/claude-opus-4-6 is now configured as an optional model, though it can’t be used yet due to Anthropic’s billing policy change. Once credits are activated, it should work fine. The main pitfall was the asdf shim conflicting with the standalone Claude CLI install — version managers’ shim mechanisms can cause unexpected interception when multiple tools coexist. Worth watching out for.

Claude Code 2.1.92 Changelog Deep Dive: All 21 Changes Explained

Apr 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Analysis date: 2026-04-04 Source: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

I. New Features (Added)

Section titled “I. New Features (Added)”

1. forceRemoteSettingsRefresh Policy Setting

Section titled “1. forceRemoteSettingsRefresh Policy Setting”

Background Enterprise/team admins distribute policies via managed-settings.json. Previously, these were cached in remote-settings.json — if a remote fetch failed on startup, the CLI would fall back to stale cache. Revoked permissions could remain effective, creating a security window.

Use Cases

  • Finance/healthcare compliance: revoked permissions must enforce immediately
  • SOC2/ISO27001 audits requiring “fail-closed” rather than “fail-open” policies

Example

CLI blocks on startup waiting for successful remote config fetch → proceeds only on success; exits on failure (fail-closed).

Notes

  • Unstable networks will prevent CLI startup — suited for corporate intranets, not offline dev
  • Only relevant for Team/Enterprise admins

Related Changes

  • 2.1.83: Added managed-settings.d/ sharded policy directory
  • 2.1.80: Fixed managed-settings not applied on startup
  • 2.1.78: Fixed PreToolUse hooks bypassing deny rules

Comparisons

  • Codex CLI: No enterprise policy management
  • Gemini CLI: Has enforcedAuthType (v0.5.0) but no fail-closed policy refresh

Trend: Enterprise CLI coding tools moving toward MDM-style policy compliance.

2. Interactive Bedrock Setup Wizard

Section titled “2. Interactive Bedrock Setup Wizard”

Background AWS Bedrock configuration was a pain point — manually setting multiple environment variables.

Use Cases

  • Enterprise users accessing Claude through AWS Bedrock
  • New employee onboarding without reading docs

Example Launch Claude Code → select “3rd-party platform” → enter wizard:

  1. Choose AWS auth method (SSO / Access Key / IAM Role)
  2. Configure Region
  3. Validate credentials
  4. Select/pin model

Notes

  • Only available from login screen; use claude auth logout to re-enter
  • Model pinning matters — Bedrock model IDs differ from Anthropic API format

Related Changes

  • 2.1.84: Added model capability override env vars for 3P
  • 2.1.86: Improved Bedrock/Vertex prompt cache hit rates
  • 2.1.83: Improved Bedrock SDK cold start latency

Comparisons

  • Codex CLI: OpenAI API only
  • Gemini CLI: Google Cloud only — simpler but no multi-cloud

Trend: Multi-cloud LLM access becoming enterprise must-have.

3. /cost Now Shows Per-Model and Cache-Hit Breakdown

Section titled “3. /cost Now Shows Per-Model and Cache-Hit Breakdown”

Background Previously /cost only showed total spend. No visibility into per-model costs or cache hit rates.

Use Cases

  • Subscription users optimizing token distribution
  • Deciding whether to adjust effort levels

Example

Notes

  • Only for subscription users
  • Cache-hit percentage helps decide whether to /clear

Related Changes

  • 2.1.89: Fixed sub-agent usage not counted in /stats
  • 2.1.84: Tokens ≥1M displayed as “1.5m”
  • 2.1.80: Added rate_limits to statusline

Comparisons

  • Codex CLI: No built-in cost tracking
  • Gemini CLI: Has --session-summary JSON but no interactive view

4. /release-notes Interactive Version Picker

Section titled “4. /release-notes Interactive Version Picker”

Previously only showed current version. Now you can browse any version’s changelog interactively.

5. Remote Control Session Names Use Hostname Prefix

Section titled “5. Remote Control Session Names Use Hostname Prefix”

Session names now default to macbook-pro-graceful-unicorn instead of just graceful-unicorn. Override with --remote-control-session-name-prefix.

6. Prompt Cache Expiration Notice (Pro Users)

Section titled “6. Prompt Cache Expiration Notice (Pro Users)”

Status bar now shows “~150K tokens will be sent uncached” when cache TTL expires. Helps decide whether to continue or /clear.

II. Bug Fixes (Fixed)

Section titled “II. Bug Fixes (Fixed)”

7. tmux Sub-Agent “Could not determine pane count” Error

Section titled “7. tmux Sub-Agent “Could not determine pane count” Error”

Fixed permanent sub-agent failure when tmux windows were manually killed or renumbered during long runs.

8. Stop Hooks False Failures and preventContinuation:true Fix

Section titled “8. Stop Hooks False Failures and preventContinuation:true Fix”

Fixed fast model ok:false incorrectly flagging hooks as failed, and preventContinuation:true semantics being lost on non-Stop hooks.

9. Streaming JSON-Encoded Field Validation Failures

Section titled “9. Streaming JSON-Encoded Field Validation Failures”

Fixed array/object fields arriving as JSON-encoded strings during streaming, causing type validation failures.

10. Extended Thinking Empty Text Blocks Causing API 400

Section titled “10. Extended Thinking Empty Text Blocks Causing API 400”

Fixed whitespace-only text blocks from extended thinking being rejected by the API.

11. Auto-Pilot Accidentally Triggering Feedback Surveys

Section titled “11. Auto-Pilot Accidentally Triggering Feedback Surveys”

Fixed automated keypresses triggering survey popups and number input conflicts with survey options.

12. Fullscreen “esc to interrupt” vs “esc to clear” Conflict

Section titled “12. Fullscreen “esc to interrupt” vs “esc to clear” Conflict”

Fixed contradictory Esc prompts appearing simultaneously during text selection.

13. Homebrew Update Channel Fix

Section titled “13. Homebrew Update Channel Fix”

Fixed brew upgrade claude-code and brew upgrade claude-code@latest using wrong release channels.

14. ctrl+e Multi-Line Edit Line Jump Bug

Section titled “14. ctrl+e Multi-Line Edit Line Jump Bug”

Fixed cursor jumping to next line’s end instead of staying on current line.

15. Fullscreen Duplicate Messages (DEC 2026 Terminals)

Section titled “15. Fullscreen Duplicate Messages (DEC 2026 Terminals)”

Fixed race condition in iTerm2/Ghostty causing messages to appear in two positions when scrolling.

16. “/clear to save X tokens” Incorrect Count

Section titled “18. Write Tool Diff Computation 60% Faster”

21. Linux Sandbox Restores apply-seccomp Helper

Fixed missing seccomp binary in npm/native builds that caused sandbox degradation on Linux.

VI. Comprehensive Comparison

  • Enterprise Policies: Claude Code has fail-closed + managed-settings.d; Codex CLI none; Gemini CLI has enforcedAuthType
  • Multi-Cloud: Claude Code has Bedrock + Vertex + Foundry; Codex CLI OpenAI-only; Gemini CLI Google-only

Claude Code 2.1.91 Deep Dive: Breaking Down All 13 Changes

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Analysis date: 2026-04-03 Source: Claude Code CHANGELOG.md

Claude Code 2.1.91 looks like a small patch release on paper, but it carries a surprisingly strong signal. These 13 updates span five themes at once: MCP maturity, enterprise safety, session reliability, token efficiency, and developer experience.

This article walks through each change, the problem behind it, practical use cases, caveats, related changes in earlier versions, and how it compares with Codex CLI and Gemini CLI.

Why 2.1.91 matters more than it looks

Section titled “Why 2.1.91 matters more than it looks”

At first glance, this is just a short changelog. In reality, it reveals several clear product directions:

  1. MCP is moving from “works” to “scales.”
  2. Enterprise controls are getting stricter and more explicit.
  3. Session durability remains a major engineering battlefield.
  4. Token economics are now being optimized at the tool-protocol level.

Let’s go change by change.

1. MCP large-result persistence override

Section titled “1. MCP large-result persistence override”

Change: Claude Code now supports _meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"], allowing an MCP server to request a higher result retention cap of up to 500K characters.

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code has default truncation limits for MCP tool results, roughly around 25K characters, to avoid flooding the context window. That works fine for small outputs, but it becomes painful when an MCP tool returns something genuinely important and naturally large, such as a database schema, a repository index, or a large search result.

Before this release, MCP server authors had no direct way to say: “this result is large, but it is also important—please keep more of it.”

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Database schema inspection: a Postgres MCP server returns the full schema for 200+ tables
  • Code search: a repository-wide search returns many relevant code blocks that should remain intact
  • Document retrieval: an MCP-based RAG server returns several long but highly relevant documents

Technical detail

Section titled “Technical detail”

The MCP server can return metadata like this:

This is an Anthropic-specific vendor extension, built on top of the MCP _meta extension mechanism.

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • The cap is still finite: 500K is the upper bound
  • Larger results consume more context and may trigger compaction sooner
  • MCP servers must opt in explicitly

Related changes in earlier versions

Section titled “Related changes in earlier versions”
VersionRelated change
2.1.84MCP tool descriptions capped at 2KB
2.1.86Better prompt cache hit rate by removing dynamic tool-description content
2.1.89Fixed MCP error truncation to only the first content block

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductLarge MCP result handling
Claude CodeServer-side override via _meta, up to 500K
Codex CLINo MCP support; uses native function calling
Gemini CLISupports MCP-style extensions, but no equivalent server-side size override

Trend

Section titled “Trend”

This is the kind of capability that may eventually become standardized in MCP itself. For now, Anthropic is moving faster through vendor extensions.

2. disableSkillShellExecution for enterprise safety

Section titled “2. disableSkillShellExecution for enterprise safety”

Change: A new setting disables inline shell execution in skills, custom slash commands, and plugin commands.

Background

Section titled “Background”

Skills are powerful, but that power comes with risk. If a skill can execute shell inline, then an untrusted or poorly audited skill can become a serious safety problem in enterprise environments.

This release finally adds a clean master switch.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Enterprise IT policy: centrally disable shell execution in third-party skills
  • CI/CD environments: reduce execution surface area in automated runs
  • Compliance-heavy organizations: ensure that all execution paths remain explicit and auditable

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • This only blocks inline shell execution inside skills/commands/plugins
  • It does not disable ordinary user-requested Bash tool calls
  • Existing skills that depend on inline shell execution may stop working

Related changes

Section titled “Related changes”
VersionRelated change
2.1.83managed-settings.d/ for modular enterprise policy
2.1.85Org policy can block plugin installation
2.1.78CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB to remove credentials from subprocesses

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductControl model
Claude CodeExplicit disableSkillShellExecution switch
Codex CLIPlugin sandbox model with explicit permissions
Gemini CLIFine-grained Policy Engine allowlisting

This is a strong signal that Claude Code is continuing its shift from a hacker-friendly terminal tool toward a more controlled enterprise execution surface.

3. Multi-line prompts in deep links

Section titled “3. Multi-line prompts in deep links”

Change: claude-cli://open?q= now accepts encoded newlines (%0A) in prompts.

Why this matters

Section titled “Why this matters”

This sounds tiny, but it actually matters a lot for integration. Once deep links can carry multi-line prompts, Claude Code becomes easier to embed inside IDEs, documentation, tutorials, browser tools, and automation workflows.

Example

Section titled “Example”

Related changes

Section titled “Related changes”
VersionRelated change
2.1.85Deep-link query length raised to 5,000 chars
2.1.84Deep links open in the preferred terminal
2.1.89Fixed claude-cli:// not opening on macOS
2.1.83Added disableDeepLinkRegistration

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”

Deep-link support remains a distinctive Claude Code advantage. Neither Codex CLI nor Gemini CLI currently has a comparable CLI protocol ecosystem.

4. Plugins can ship executables in bin/

Section titled “4. Plugins can ship executables in bin/”

Change: Plugins can now include executables under bin/ and invoke them as bare commands from Bash.

What this unlocks

Section titled “What this unlocks”

This moves plugins closer to being real, self-contained tool bundles rather than just wrappers around prompts, hooks, or MCP declarations.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • A custom linter bundled as bin/my-linter
  • A schema/code generator packaged with the plugin
  • A workflow plugin that ships specialized infra tools

Caveats

Section titled “Caveats”
  • Files under bin/ still need correct executable permissions
  • Existing permission policies still apply
  • 2.1.86 recently fixed marketplace-plugin permission issues on macOS/Linux

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductPlugin executable model
Claude CodeNative bin/ support for bare-command invocation
Codex CLIPlugin system supports custom tools, but with a different model
Gemini CLIExtensions are generally MCP/npm oriented, not bin/ oriented

This is a meaningful step toward a more serious plugin ecosystem.

5. Fixed transcript-chain breaks on --resume

Section titled “5. Fixed transcript-chain breaks on --resume”

Change: Claude Code fixed cases where async transcript write failures could silently break conversation history during --resume.

Why this is dangerous

Section titled “Why this is dangerous”

This is the worst kind of bug in an agent system: not a loud crash, but a silent loss of history. Users believe a session has been restored, but the context chain is already broken.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • Resuming a long coding session the next day and finding part of the context gone
  • Recovering deferred tools in SDK or CI flows with missing state
  • Containerized remote sessions losing transcript integrity after restarts

Why --resume keeps showing up in the changelog

Section titled “Why --resume keeps showing up in the changelog”

Because it sits at the intersection of several hard problems:

  • tool/result consistency
  • async persistence timing
  • large-session durability
  • old-transcript compatibility
  • remote container lifecycle issues

Related fixes across versions

Section titled “Related fixes across versions”
VersionRelated fix
2.1.90Prompt-cache miss on --resume
2.1.89Older-transcript crashes; -p --resume hangs
2.1.86Missing tool_result chain restoration
2.1.85SDK history loss on resume
2.1.83Remote-session history loss after restart
2.1.77Silent truncation of recent history

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductSession recovery model
Claude CodeFull transcript-chain restore via --resume
Codex CLISimpler session-file restore
Gemini CLI30-day history plus /rewind

Claude Code’s system is more ambitious, but that also means more complexity and more repair work.

6. Fixed cmd+delete across modern terminals

Section titled “6. Fixed cmd+delete across modern terminals”

Change: cmd+delete now correctly deletes to the start of the line in iTerm2, kitty, WezTerm, Ghostty, and Windows Terminal.

This is not a glamorous fix, but it’s exactly the sort of thing power users feel every day.

Root cause

Section titled “Root cause”

Different terminals emit different escape sequences for the same shortcut. Claude Code had only covered part of that landscape.

Fallback

Section titled “Fallback”

Ctrl+U remains the reliable readline-style fallback.

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”

All three products face terminal compatibility friction. Claude Code is doing an especially thorough job of adapting to newer terminals like Ghostty and kitty.

7. Fixed plan mode in remote sessions

Section titled “7. Fixed plan mode in remote sessions”

Change: Claude Code fixed plan mode losing track of its plan file in remote sessions after container restarts.

What was happening

Section titled “What was happening”

Once the plan file path was lost, two bad things followed:

  1. Editing the plan triggered unnecessary permission prompts
  2. The plan-approval modal showed up empty

Impacted environments

Section titled “Impacted environments”
  • Remote Control sessions
  • Dev Containers
  • cloud IDEs such as Codespaces/Gitpod-like environments

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”
ProductPlan mode + remote
Claude CodeMature plan mode plus remote control, now more reliable
Codex CLINo equivalent plan mode
Gemini CLIPlan mode by default, but no comparable remote-session stack

This fix highlights that Claude Code is increasingly operating as a persistent cross-device work environment, not just a local CLI.

8. Fixed schema validation for permissions.defaultMode: "auto"

Section titled “8. Fixed schema validation for permissions.defaultMode: "auto"”

Change: JSON schema validation now correctly accepts permissions.defaultMode: "auto".

This is a “small but important” fix. Even if the setting worked at runtime, a schema mismatch damages trust:

  • editors show red squiggles
  • teams doubt the docs
  • config rollout becomes noisier than it should be

For enterprise deployment, schema correctness matters more than many teams realize.

9. Fixed Windows rollback-copy cleanup

Section titled “9. Fixed Windows rollback-copy cleanup”

Change: Windows version cleanup no longer deletes the rollback copy of the active version.

This is classic reliability plumbing. Nobody notices it when it works, but when rollback is needed, it becomes critical.

Claude Code’s Windows installation model is heavier than npm-only tools like Codex CLI or Gemini CLI, so this kind of fix matters more in its ecosystem.

10. /feedback now explains why it is unavailable

Section titled “10. /feedback now explains why it is unavailable”

Change: /feedback no longer simply disappears; it now explains why it cannot be used.

This is a very good UX improvement. “Unavailable with explanation” is much better than “seems to have vanished.” That matters especially for:

  • enterprise deployments
  • third-party provider setups
  • proxy and managed environments

This reduces the chance that users interpret an intentional limitation as a broken product.

11. Improved /claude-api skill guidance

Section titled “11. Improved /claude-api skill guidance”

Change: Anthropic expanded the built-in /claude-api guidance around agent design patterns, including tool-surface choices, context management, and caching strategy.

This looks like a docs tweak, but it actually matters a lot. The competitive edge in 2026 is no longer just model quality. It is increasingly about:

  • how many tools you expose
  • how you control context growth
  • how you use caching well
  • when to split or avoid subagents

Anthropic is effectively productizing its own operational experience into reusable guidance.

12. Faster stripAnsi on Bun

Section titled “12. Faster stripAnsi on Bun”

Change: Claude Code now routes ANSI stripping through native Bun.stripANSI when running on Bun.

This is the kind of high-frequency micro-optimization that compounds over time. Each call is small, but log-heavy workflows invoke this path constantly.

Practical scenarios

Section titled “Practical scenarios”
  • long build logs
  • package installs
  • test runs with large terminal output

Gemini CLI and Codex CLI still primarily follow Node.js-first paths, so this kind of Bun-specific optimization is a notable differentiator.

13. Shorter old_string anchors in the Edit tool

Section titled “13. Shorter old_string anchors in the Edit tool”

Change: The Edit tool now uses shorter old_string anchors while still preserving uniqueness, reducing output tokens.

This is one of the most revealing changes in the whole release.

Why it matters

Section titled “Why it matters”

It shows that Claude Code is now optimizing token costs at the tool protocol level, not just at the prompt or model level.

In agent systems, cost comes from more than inference:

  • verbose tool schemas
  • repetitive file context
  • long edit anchors
  • redundant tool I/O

Once a team starts optimizing anchor length, it means they are thinking in terms of “token compound interest” across thousands of repeated actions.

Related token-efficiency improvements

Section titled “Related token-efficiency improvements”
VersionOptimization
2.1.86Compact line-number formatting in Read
2.1.86Lower token cost for @ mentions
2.1.89Edit can act on files previously viewed via sed -n

Comparison

Section titled “Comparison”

Claude Codeold_string anchor model, now optimized

Final take: the five signals of 2.1.91

Section titled “Final take: the five signals of 2.1.91”

If you zoom out, Claude Code 2.1.91 sends five clear signals:

Claude Code’s strongest advantage right now is not one flashy feature. It is systems engineering for agents.

MCP, permissions, transcript recovery, remote workflows, and token efficiency are all converging into something more durable: a developer operating system for long-running AI-assisted work, not just a terminal coding assistant.
