Claude Code 2.1.89 Changelog Deep Analysis

Apr 1, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Release date: Late 2025 – Early 2026 (estimated) Analysis date: 2026-04-01

This article dissects every change in Claude Code 2.1.89, analyzing the problem context, use cases with examples, and caveats, while drawing lateral comparisons with Codex CLI and Gemini CLI, and closing with a look at evolution trends.

Table of Contents

Section titled “Table of Contents”
  1. New Features (Added)
  2. Bug Fixes (Fixed)
  3. UX Improvements (Improved)
  4. Behavioral Changes (Changed)
  5. Miscellaneous & Easter Eggs
  6. Summary & Trends

1. New Features

Section titled “1. New Features”

1.1 "defer" Decision for PreToolUse Hooks

Section titled “1.1 "defer" Decision for PreToolUse Hooks”

What changed: The PreToolUse hook can now return "defer" as a permission decision. Headless sessions (-p mode) pause at that tool call, and the user later resumes with -p --resume, at which point the hook is re-evaluated.

Problem context: In CI/CD or automation pipelines, Claude Code runs in headless mode (-p). Previously, hooks could only return allow or deny. When human approval was needed (e.g., executing a dangerous command or writing to production config), you had to either allow everything or deny everything—no middle ground.

Use cases & examples:

In a CI pipeline, Claude Code encounters rm -rf build/ and pauses. After an ops engineer reviews the action:

The hook re-evaluates (it can now check an external approval system’s status) and decides to allow or deny.

Caveats:

  • --resume would hang if the deferred tool input exceeded 64KB or lacked a deferred marker (this release also fixes that issue).
  • You need to design a proper polling/callback mechanism for external approval state.

Cross-tool comparison:

DimensionClaude CodeCodex CLIGemini CLI
Hook systemPreToolUse/PostToolUse with allow/deny/deferNo hook system; relies on global --approval-mode switchNo hook system
Pause/Resumedefer + --resumeNot supportedNot supported
CI integrationFirst-class citizenBasic supportLimited

Trend: This signals Claude Code’s evolution toward a “composable AI Agent runtime”—not just a CLI tool, but an execution engine that can be embedded in enterprise approval workflows. We may eventually see webhook-callback-style defer (no manual resume needed).

1.2 CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1 Flicker-Free Rendering

Section titled “1.2 CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1 Flicker-Free Rendering”

What changed: A new environment variable enables alt-screen-based flicker-free rendering with virtualized scroll-back.

Problem context: Claude Code’s TUI (terminal UI) tends to flicker and jitter during long streaming output, especially under iTerm2/tmux. This happens because the default main-screen rendering mode causes each redraw to affect the scroll buffer.

Use cases:

Ideal for:

  • Users running Claude Code inside tmux
  • Users on low-refresh-rate terminal emulators
  • Extended sessions (coding marathons)

Caveats:

  • In alt-screen mode, session content is not preserved in the terminal scroll buffer after exit (similar to how vim restores the screen on quit).
  • Marked as “opt-in,” indicating it’s not mature enough to be the default and may have edge-case compatibility issues.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Ink (React for CLI) rendering with built-in alt-screen; less flickering but lower customizability.
  • Gemini CLI: Python-based Rich/Textual rendering; moderate flicker control.

Trend: Terminal AI tools are moving from “functional” to “polished.” Rendering quality is becoming a core UX differentiator. Alt-screen with full virtual scrolling may become the default in the future.

1.3 PermissionDenied Hook

Section titled “1.3 PermissionDenied Hook”

What changed: A new PermissionDenied hook fires after the auto-mode classifier rejects an operation. Returning {retry: true} lets the model retry.

Problem context: In auto mode, Claude Code has a safety classifier that automatically rejects operations deemed dangerous. But sometimes these are false positives, especially when command semantics are complex. Previously, users could only manually retry or switch to manual mode.

Use cases: A custom hook script checks whether the rejected command is on a whitelist:

For example, docker compose down might be misclassified as a dangerous delete command—the hook can automatically allow a retry.

Caveats:

  • retry: true just tells the model it can retry; it doesn’t bypass permissions—the model may take a different approach.
  • Overusing this hook undermines the safety classifier’s protective value.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Has three modes (suggest / auto-edit / full-auto), no fine-grained hooks.
  • Gemini CLI: Uses Google’s safety filters with no user-customizable recovery mechanism.

1.4 Named Subagents in @ Mentions

Section titled “1.4 Named Subagents in @ Mentions”

What changed: Named subagents now appear in @-mention autocomplete suggestions.

Problem context: Claude Code supports background subagents for task execution. Previously, users could only manage subagents through /agents or the API—referencing them in conversation was inconvenient.

Use cases: While coding, you’ve launched a background subagent for testing:

The @ autocomplete dropdown now shows named subagents for direct reference.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No subagent support.
  • Gemini CLI: No subagent support.

Trend: Multi-agent orchestration is evolving from a “background concept” to a “first-class interactive object.” In the future, @ may unify references to files, tools, agents, and MCP resources.

1.5 Non-Blocking MCP Connections

Section titled “1.5 Non-Blocking MCP Connections”

What changed: MCP_CONNECTION_NONBLOCKING=true completely skips MCP connection waiting in -p mode; additionally, --mcp-config server connections are capped at 5 seconds.

Problem context: MCP (Model Context Protocol) server connections can be slow (network latency, slow server startup). In CI scenarios where only partial MCP capabilities are needed, waiting for all servers to connect significantly delays startup.

Use cases:

Caveats:

  • In non-blocking mode, if the model calls an MCP tool that hasn’t connected yet, it will fail.
  • The 5-second timeout may be too short for cold-starting SSE servers.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No MCP support.
  • Gemini CLI: Supports MCP but has no non-blocking option; failed connections are simply skipped.

Trend: MCP connection management is moving toward a “progressive readiness” model—start first, connect tools on demand, rather than requiring everything to be ready at launch.

1.6 Notifications & Retry for Auto Mode Rejections

Section titled “1.6 Notifications & Retry for Auto Mode Rejections”

What changed: Commands rejected in auto mode now display a notification and appear in /permissions → Recent tab, where you can press r to retry.

Problem context: Previously, auto mode silently swallowed rejections—users might not know why a task didn’t complete.

Use cases: Claude Code in auto mode attempts git push --force and gets rejected. A notification pops up in the terminal: “Permission denied: git push —force.” The user opens /permissions → Recent, sees the record, and presses r to allow and retry.

Caveats:

  • This balances security with usability—keeping users informed without interrupting their workflow.

2. Bug Fixes

Section titled “2. Bug Fixes”

2.1 Permission Rules for Symlinked Paths

Section titled “2.1 Permission Rules for Symlinked Paths”

What changed: Edit(//path/**) and Read(//path/**) rules now check the resolved symlink target path rather than the requested path.

Problem context: Security vulnerability: an attacker could create a symlink /safe/link → /etc/passwd. If permission rules only checked /safe/**, protected files could be read/written through the symlink.

Use cases:

Caveats:

  • If your project has legitimate symlinks pointing to external directories, you’ll need to add explicit allow rules.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses sandboxing (Docker/seatbelt) to restrict file access at the OS level, not relying on path rules.
  • Gemini CLI: Simpler permission model with no fine-grained path rules.

2.2 Voice Mode Fixes (Multiple)

Section titled “2.2 Voice Mode Fixes (Multiple)”

What changed:

  1. Fixed push-to-talk not activating with certain modifier key combinations
  2. Fixed voice mode reporting “WebSocket upgrade rejected with HTTP 101” on Windows
  3. Fixed voice mode failing to request microphone permissions on macOS Apple Silicon

Problem context: Voice mode is a differentiating feature for Claude Code, but cross-platform compatibility has been a persistent pain point: Windows handles WebSocket differently, macOS Apple Silicon has a unique permissions model, and different terminal emulators handle key bindings differently.

Caveats:

  • Voice mode is still experimental and may not work in SSH/remote sessions.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No voice mode.
  • Gemini CLI: No voice mode.

2.3 Windows CRLF and Markdown Hard Break Fixes

Section titled “2.3 Windows CRLF and Markdown Hard Break Fixes”

What changed: Edit/Write tools no longer double up CRLF on Windows (causing double blank lines) and no longer strip Markdown hard breaks (trailing double spaces).

Problem context: Windows uses \r\n as line endings. If the tool converts \n to \r\n but the input is already \r\n, it becomes \r\r\n, producing double blank lines. Meanwhile, trailing double spaces in Markdown (which represent <br>) were being incorrectly trimmed.

Use cases: Editing .md files on Windows: before the fix, blank lines doubled on every save; Markdown table alignment and other scenarios requiring trailing spaces were broken.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Also uses patch-based editing, but runs in a Docker sandbox (Linux), sidestepping CRLF issues.
  • Gemini CLI: Uses Python’s file handling under the hood, which handles line endings more maturely.

2.4 StructuredOutput Schema Caching Bug

Section titled “2.4 StructuredOutput Schema Caching Bug”

What changed: Fixed a StructuredOutput schema cache bug that caused ~50% failure rate when using multiple schemas.

Problem context: The --json-schema feature lets Claude Code produce structured output. When different schemas were used within the same session, a flawed cache key caused the wrong schema to be returned, failing JSON validation.

Use cases:

Caveats:

  • A 50% failure rate means any automation pipeline relying on multiple schemas was unreliable before this fix.

2.5 Memory Leak in Long Sessions

Section titled “2.5 Memory Leak in Long Sessions”

What changed: Fixed a memory leak caused by large JSON inputs being retained as LRU cache keys.

Problem context: The LRU cache used the full JSON string of input content as its key. When inputs were large (e.g., reading large file contents), these strings stayed in memory and were never garbage collected. In extended sessions (e.g., 8-hour coding marathons), the Node.js process memory would climb continuously.

Use cases: After several hours of continuous Claude Code use and reading multiple large files, process memory grows from 300MB to 2GB+, and the terminal starts lagging.

Caveats:

  • For long sessions, periodically using /clear or /compact is recommended.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses React/Ink rendering; also exhibits memory growth but manifests differently.
  • Gemini CLI: Python runtime with a different GC strategy; long sessions may have similar issues.

2.6 Crash When Deleting Messages from >50MB Session Files

Section titled “2.6 Crash When Deleting Messages from >50MB Session Files”

What changed: Fixed a crash when deleting messages from session files exceeding 50MB.

Problem context: Session transcript files grow with conversation length. Sessions that heavily use tools (especially reading large files) can easily exceed 50MB. The full-file parse-and-rewrite operation when deleting messages caused out-of-memory errors or timeout crashes on oversized files.

2.7 LSP Server Zombie State Fix

Section titled “2.7 LSP Server Zombie State Fix”

What changed: After an LSP server crash, it no longer enters a zombie state; instead, it automatically restarts on the next request.

Problem context: Claude Code integrates LSP (Language Server Protocol) for code intelligence (go-to-definition, type checking, etc.). When an LSP server crashed, it previously entered an unusable state, silently failing all subsequent LSP operations until the user manually restarted the session.

Use cases: In a TypeScript project, editing a massive .d.ts file causes tsserver to OOM and crash. Before the fix, you had to exit and reenter Claude Code; after the fix, the next LSP call auto-recovers.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No LSP integration.
  • Gemini CLI: No LSP integration.
  • VS Code/Cursor: Auto-restarting LSP is standard.

Trend: Claude Code is approaching IDE-level robustness.

2.8 CJK/Emoji Prompt History Loss

Section titled “2.8 CJK/Emoji Prompt History Loss”

What changed: Fixed prompt history entries containing CJK or emoji being silently discarded at 4KB boundaries in ~/.claude/history.jsonl.

Problem context: The JSONL file is read in 4KB chunks. CJK characters and emoji use multi-byte UTF-8 encoding (3–4 bytes). When a character straddles a 4KB boundary, it gets truncated, causing JSON parse failure and the entire record being silently dropped.

Use cases: Chinese/Japanese/Korean users frequently using Claude Code would find their prompt history missing (pressing the up arrow couldn’t find previous commands).

Caveats:

  • This bug affected a large number of Asian users; the fix is significant.
  • Similar UTF-8 boundary bugs exist in many tools.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses Node.js readline; CJK handling is delegated to system libraries.
  • Gemini CLI: Python’s Unicode handling is relatively mature, though similar boundary issues may still occur.

2.9 Inaccurate /stats Token Counts

Section titled “2.9 Inaccurate /stats Token Counts”

What changed: Fixed /stats not counting subagent token usage, and fixed loss of 30+ day historical data when the statistics cache format changed.

Problem context: Users rely on /stats to monitor API usage and costs. Missing subagent usage means significantly underestimating actual consumption, especially for heavy background agent users.

2.10 --resume and --continue Recovery Issues

Section titled “2.10 --resume and --continue Recovery Issues”

What changed: Fixed -p --resume hanging when deferred tool input exceeds 64KB or lacks a deferred marker, and fixed --continue not restoring deferred tools.

Problem context: Companion fix for the defer feature in §1.1—multiple edge cases existed in the resume path when defer was first introduced.

2.11 macOS Deep Links Fix

Section titled “2.11 macOS Deep Links Fix”

What changed: Fixed claude-cli:// deep links not opening on macOS.

Use cases: Clicking a claude-cli://open?q=... link in a webpage to open Claude Code in the terminal with a pre-filled prompt. Commonly used in documentation, tutorials, and team sharing.

2.12 MCP Error Truncation Fix

Section titled “2.12 MCP Error Truncation Fix”

What changed: MCP tools returning multi-element error content no longer show only the first content block.

Problem context: MCP servers may return complex error information (e.g., error description + stack trace + suggested fix across multiple content blocks). After truncation, users could only see “something went wrong” without the critical diagnostic details.

2.13 System Context Loss When Sending Images via SDK

Section titled “2.13 System Context Loss When Sending Images via SDK”

What changed: Fixed skill reminders and other system context being dropped when sending messages containing images through the SDK.

Problem context: In the SDK’s message serialization, the special handling path for images missed the system context injection step.

2.14 Hook Path Normalization

Section titled “2.14 Hook Path Normalization”

What changed: PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks now provide an absolute file_path for Write/Edit/Read tools.

Problem context: Previously, the path might be relative, requiring hook scripts to resolve it themselves—an error-prone process. The fix aligns behavior with the documentation.

2.15 Autocompact Infinite Loop Fix ⭐

Section titled “2.15 Autocompact Infinite Loop Fix ⭐”

What changed: When context refills immediately after compaction (3 consecutive times), the system now stops and reports an actionable error instead of looping infinitely and burning API calls.

Problem context: This was a severe cost and usability bug. When project configuration caused large amounts of context to be injected (e.g., deeply nested CLAUDE.md files, verbose skill descriptions), compaction would clear them only for them to be re-injected immediately, triggering another compaction—an infinite loop. Each compaction is an API call, potentially consuming enormous amounts of tokens without the user’s knowledge.

Use cases: In a large monorepo with multiple layers of nested CLAUDE.md files, each compaction re-injects all of them, pushing token count right back to the threshold. After dozens of cycles, the user discovers their API usage has skyrocketed.

Caveats:

  • If you encounter this error, check for excessive CLAUDE.md nesting or overly verbose skill descriptions.
  • Understand this fix in conjunction with §2.17 (CLAUDE.md duplicate injection).

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: No auto-compact feature; when context is full, it simply errors out.
  • Gemini CLI: Different context management strategy; no equivalent loop issue.

Trend: Automatic context management is essential for long-session usability, but needs smarter strategies (e.g., incremental compaction, selective retention, importance scoring).

2.16 Prompt Cache Hit Rate Degradation Fix

Section titled “2.16 Prompt Cache Hit Rate Degradation Fix”

What changed: Fixed prompt cache misses in long sessions caused by tool schema byte changes.

Problem context: Anthropic’s API prompt cache relies on prefix matching. If tool schemas change slightly during a session (e.g., an MCP tool dynamically updates its description), the entire prompt prefix is invalidated, causing a cache miss. Every request must then reprocess the full context, dramatically increasing latency and cost.

Caveats:

  • This is a “hidden cost” bug—users might just feel “things got slower” without realizing it’s a cache miss.

2.17 Nested CLAUDE.md Duplicate Injection

Section titled “2.17 Nested CLAUDE.md Duplicate Injection”

What changed: Fixed nested CLAUDE.md files being injected dozens of times during long sessions with multiple file reads.

Problem context: Claude Code automatically discovers and loads CLAUDE.md files at every level of the project. In long sessions, as file operations accumulate, the deduplication logic breaks down, and the same CLAUDE.md might be added to context 20–30 times.

Use cases: A monorepo where each package has its own CLAUDE.md:

During a long session with frequent cross-package operations, all CLAUDE.md files get re-injected with each operation.

2.18 --resume Compatibility Crash

Section titled “2.18 --resume Compatibility Crash”

What changed: Fixed --resume crashing when the transcript contains tool results from older CLI versions or interrupted writes.

Problem context: Rapid CLI iteration means tool result serialization formats change. Resuming old sessions may encounter format incompatibilities.

2.19 Misleading “Rate limit reached” Error

Section titled “2.19 Misleading “Rate limit reached” Error”

What changed: When the API actually returns an entitlement error, the misleading “Rate limit reached” message is replaced with the real error and an actionable prompt.

Problem context: Users seeing “Rate limit reached” assume it’s temporary throttling and wait to retry. But the actual cause might be:

  • Plan doesn’t support the feature
  • API key lacks access to the model
  • Organization quota is exhausted

After the fix, messages like “Your plan does not include access to claude-opus-4. Upgrade at…” are displayed instead.

2.20 Hook if Conditions Not Matching Compound Commands

Section titled “2.20 Hook if Conditions Not Matching Compound Commands”

What changed: Fixed hook if conditions not matching compound commands like ls && git push or commands with environment variable prefixes like FOO=bar git push.

Problem context:

Previously, git push would match, but ls && git push and FOO=bar git push wouldn’t. Attack vector: a model could bypass hooks by chaining commands.

2.21 Devanagari and Other Combining Mark Text Truncation

Section titled “2.21 Devanagari and Other Combining Mark Text Truncation”

What changed: Fixed Hindi and other scripts using combining marks being truncated in assistant output.

Problem context: In complex writing systems like Devanagari, a single visual character may consist of a base character plus multiple combining marks (vowel signs, virama, etc.). Truncating by byte or code point may break in the middle of combining marks, causing garbled text or data loss.

Caveats:

  • Internationalization support is a long-tail need for CLI tools, but it’s a critical issue for specific user populations.

2.22 Windows-Specific Fixes

Section titled “2.22 Windows-Specific Fixes”

This release includes multiple Windows fixes, reflecting increased commitment to Windows platform support:

  1. Shift+Enter submits instead of inserting newline — Key code handling difference in Windows Terminal Preview 1.25
  2. PowerShell stderr false failure reports — Commands like git push write progress to stderr; PowerShell 5.1 treats this as failure
  3. Edit tool OOM on >1GiB files — Large files loaded entirely into memory

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Windows support via WSL/Docker; limited native Windows support.
  • Gemini CLI: Python-based cross-platform; decent native Windows support but weaker terminal interaction.

2.23 Streaming Render Jitter in iTerm2 + tmux

Section titled “2.23 Streaming Render Jitter in iTerm2 + tmux”

What changed: Fixed periodic UI jitter during streaming output when using iTerm2 inside tmux.

Problem context: tmux and terminal emulators communicate via escape sequences. High-frequency refreshes from streaming output conflict with tmux’s pane redraw mechanism, causing visible jitter.

2.24 Other Terminal Rendering Fixes

Section titled “2.24 Other Terminal Rendering Fixes”
  • Collapsed search/read group badges duplicated — UI components duplicated during parallel tool calls
  • Notifications not clearing promptly — invalidates field not working
  • Prompt briefly disappearing after submission — Background message race condition
  • Main-screen rendering artifacts — Residual artifacts after layout shift

3. UX Improvements

Section titled “3. UX Improvements”

3.1 Tool Summary Optimization

Section titled “3.1 Tool Summary Optimization”

What changed: ls/tree/du now display “Listed N directories” instead of “Read N files.”

Problem context: Semantic accuracy—listing directories isn’t “reading files,” and the previous wording was confusing for users.

3.2 Stale-Edit Warning for Bash Tool ⭐

Section titled “3.2 Stale-Edit Warning for Bash Tool ⭐”

What changed: The Bash tool now warns when a formatter/linter command modifies a file that was previously read.

Problem context: Typical scenario:

  1. Claude Code reads app.tsx
  2. Claude Code runs prettier --write app.tsx (formatting modifies the file)
  3. Claude Code generates an edit based on step 1’s content → overwrites prettier’s changes

After the fix, step 2 warns “This command modified a file you previously read,” prompting the model to re-read.

Caveats:

  • This is a clever heuristic—detecting whether a command modified a known file.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Uses git diff to detect changes but doesn’t proactively warn.
  • Gemini CLI: No equivalent mechanism.

3.3 @ Mention Sorting Optimization

Section titled “3.3 @ Mention Sorting Optimization”

What changed: Source files now rank higher than same-named MCP resources in mention autocomplete.

Problem context: As MCP resources multiply, the completion list can be overwhelmed by MCP resources. In most cases, users want to reference local files.

3.4 PowerShell Version-Specific Guidance

Section titled “3.4 PowerShell Version-Specific Guidance”

What changed: The PowerShell tool now provides different syntax guidance based on version (5.1 vs 7+).

Problem context: PS 5.1 (built into Windows) and PS 7+ (cross-platform) have significant syntax differences (e.g., ??= operator, ForEach-Object -Parallel are only available in 7+).

4. Behavioral Changes

Section titled “4. Behavioral Changes”

4.1 Edit Tool No Longer Requires Prior Read

Section titled “4.1 Edit Tool No Longer Requires Prior Read”

What changed: Files previously viewed via Bash’s sed -n or cat can now be edited directly without first using the Read tool.

Problem context: Previously, the Edit tool required a file to have been read by the Read tool first (for version validation). But if the model had viewed file contents through Bash and then called Edit, it would error out demanding a Read first—wasting a tool call and tokens.

Caveats:

  • Reduces unnecessary tool calls, improving efficiency.

4.2 Oversized Hook Output Stored to Disk

Section titled “4.2 Oversized Hook Output Stored to Disk”

What changed: Hook output exceeding 50K characters is stored to a disk file; only the file path and a preview are injected into context.

Problem context: Malicious or poorly designed hooks may produce massive output. Injecting it directly into context would:

  1. Rapidly fill the context window
  2. Waste tokens
  3. Potentially trigger the autocompact infinite loop

4.3 cleanupPeriodDays: 0 Validation Error

Section titled “4.3 cleanupPeriodDays: 0 Validation Error”

What changed: Setting this to 0 now throws a validation error; previously, it silently disabled transcript persistence.

Problem context: Users might set it to 0 thinking it means “unlimited” (a common off-by-one semantic), when the actual effect is “never retain”—causing all session history to be lost.

4.4 Thinking Summaries No Longer Generated by Default

Section titled “4.4 Thinking Summaries No Longer Generated by Default”

What changed: Interactive sessions no longer generate thinking summaries by default; you can restore them with showThinkingSummaries: true.

Problem context: Thinking summaries display a digest of the model’s reasoning process to the user. They add token consumption and latency, and most users don’t need them—they’re only useful when debugging model reasoning.

Cross-tool comparison:

  • Codex CLI: Has --reasoning-summary option, off by default.
  • Gemini CLI: Thinking process displayed by default, no summary concept.

4.5 /env Applies to PowerShell

Section titled “4.5 /env Applies to PowerShell”

What changed: Environment variables set via /env now also apply to PowerShell tool commands.

4.6 Simplified /usage Display

Section titled “4.6 Simplified /usage Display”

What changed: Pro and Enterprise plans no longer show the redundant “Current week (Sonnet only)” progress bar.

5. Miscellaneous & Easter Eggs

Section titled “5. Miscellaneous & Easter Eggs”

5.1 Documentation & Behavior Normalization

Section titled “5.1 Documentation & Behavior Normalization”
  • TaskCreated hook event documented along with its blocking behavior
  • Ctrl+B backgrounding preserves task notifications
  • PowerShell 5.1 parameter hardening (arguments containing double quotes + spaces trigger a prompt instead of auto-allow)
  • Pasting !command enters bash mode
  • Image pasting no longer inserts a trailing space

5.2 /buddy April Fools’ Easter Egg 🐣

Section titled “5.2 /buddy April Fools’ Easter Egg 🐣”

What changed: April 1st exclusive—hatch a little creature that watches you code.

Analysis: This reflects engineering culture. Great CLI tools should have soul and humor. /buddy is in the same vein as:

  • VS Code’s Power Mode extension
  • GitHub Copilot Chat’s emoji reactions
  • Vim’s :help holy-grail

6. Summary & Trends

Section titled “6. Summary & Trends”

6.1 Release Profile

Section titled “6.1 Release Profile”

With 60+ changes, this release reveals several clear themes:

ThemeShareRepresentative Changes
Robustness/Stability~40%Memory leak, OOM, infinite loop, zombie process fixes
Windows/Cross-platform~20%CRLF, PowerShell, Shift+Enter
Hooks/Automation~15%defer, PermissionDenied, if condition fixes
Terminal Rendering~15%Flickering, jitter, combining marks, notifications
Internationalization~10%CJK history loss, Devanagari truncation

6.2 Competitive Landscape

Section titled “6.2 Competitive Landscape”

Claude Code leads significantly in hooks and composability, evolving from a “developer tool” into an “AI Agent runtime.”

Codex CLI focuses on sandbox security and simplicity, taking an “Apple-style” minimalist approach.

Gemini CLI leverages Google’s ecosystem (Vertex AI, Cloud), pursuing an enterprise/cloud-native path.

6.3 Future Evolution Trends

Section titled “6.3 Future Evolution Trends”

  1. Agent Runtime Evolution — The combination of defer/resume/hooks is building an execution framework that can be embedded in enterprise workflows. Future possibilities include webhook callbacks, external approval system integration, and event-driven architecture.

  2. Long-Session Resilience — The autocompact loop fix, memory leak fix, and 50MB+ session support all indicate that users’ real usage pattern is “open a session and use it all day.” The future demands smarter context management: incremental compaction, importance scoring, and selective forgetting.

  3. Windows as a First-Class Citizen — Multiple consecutive releases with extensive Windows fixes and PowerShell tool additions show Claude Code is taking the Windows developer market seriously.

  4. MCP Ecosystem Maturation — Non-blocking connections, improved error handling, and timeout controls signal MCP’s transition from “experimental protocol” to “production-grade infrastructure.”

  5. Terminal UI Engineering — Alt-screen rendering, virtual scrolling, and tmux compatibility. Terminal AI tool UI quality is approaching that of GUI applications.

  6. Defense in Depth — Symlink path resolution, hook if condition hardening, and PowerShell parameter hardening. Every fix closes a potential security vulnerability.

In one sentence: Claude Code 2.1.89 is a release centered on “hardening” and “composability”—not a flashy pile of new features, but making existing capabilities truly reliable, controllable, and composable. This is the critical step from “fun tool” to “trusted infrastructure.”

5 Agent Skill Design Patterns Every ADK Developer Should Know

Mar 18, 2026
Vibe Sparking

5 Agent Skill Design Patterns Every ADK Developer Should Know

Section titled “5 Agent Skill Design Patterns Every ADK Developer Should Know”

The Format War Is Over

Section titled “The Format War Is Over”

Thirty agent tools now read the same file format. Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and more — they all parse the same SKILL.md layout with YAML frontmatter, the same directory structure, the same spec.

So why do most skills still break in production?

Because developers fixate on getting the YAML right and structuring directories. The formatting problem is solved. The challenge now is content design. The spec explains how to package a skill, but offers zero guidance on how to structure the logic inside it.

A skill that wraps FastAPI conventions operates completely differently from a four-step documentation pipeline, even though their SKILL.md files look identical on the outside. Same frontmatter. Same directories. Different reliability.

By studying how skills are built across the ecosystem — from Anthropic’s repositories to Vercel and Google’s internal guidelines — five recurring design patterns emerge. Each one answers a different architectural question. Each one comes with working ADK code.

Pattern 1: The Tool Wrapper

Section titled “Pattern 1: The Tool Wrapper”

A Tool Wrapper gives your agent on-demand context for a specific library. Instead of hardcoding API conventions into your system prompt, you package them into a skill. Your agent only loads this context when it actually works with that technology.

It’s the simplest pattern. The SKILL.md file listens for specific library keywords in the user’s prompt, dynamically loads your internal documentation from the references/ directory, and applies those rules as ground truth. This is how you distribute team coding guidelines or framework best practices directly into developer workflows.

Here’s a Tool Wrapper that teaches an agent how to write FastAPI code:

When to use it: Your task needs context injection for a specific library, framework, or internal standard.

Pattern 2: The Generator

Section titled “Pattern 2: The Generator”

While the Tool Wrapper applies knowledge, the Generator enforces consistent output. If your agent generates different document structures on every run, the Generator solves this by orchestrating a fill-in-the-blank process.

It uses two optional directories: assets/ holds your output template, and references/ holds your style guide. The instructions act as a project manager — they tell the agent to load the template, read the style guide, ask the user for missing variables, and populate the document.

When to use it: You need consistent, predictable output — API docs, commit messages, project scaffolds.

Pattern 3: The Reviewer

Section titled “Pattern 3: The Reviewer”

The Reviewer separates what to check from how to check it. Rather than writing a long system prompt detailing every code smell, you store a modular rubric inside references/review-checklist.md.

When code arrives, the agent loads the checklist and scores methodically, grouping findings by severity. Swap out a Python style checklist for an OWASP security checklist, and you get a completely different audit using the same skill infrastructure.

When to use it: You need quality scoring against a checklist — PR reviews, security audits, compliance checks.

Pattern 4: Inversion

Section titled “Pattern 4: Inversion”

Agents want to guess and generate immediately. Inversion flips this. Instead of the user driving the prompt and the agent executing, the agent interviews the user first.

The key mechanism is explicit, non-negotiable gating instructions: “DO NOT start building until all phases are complete.” The agent asks structured questions sequentially, waits for answers, and refuses to synthesize output until it has a complete picture.

When to use it: You need thorough requirements gathering before any action — project planning, architecture design, onboarding flows.

Pattern 5: The Pipeline

Section titled “Pattern 5: The Pipeline”

For complex tasks, you cannot afford skipped steps. The Pipeline enforces a strict, sequential workflow with hard checkpoints.

Instructions serve as the workflow definition. Diamond gate conditions (like requiring user approval before advancing) ensure the agent cannot bypass steps or present unvalidated results. Different reference files load only at the step where they’re needed, keeping the context window clean.

When to use it: Complex multi-step tasks where order matters and validation is required at each stage.

Choosing the Right Pattern

Section titled “Choosing the Right Pattern”

Each pattern answers a different question:

QuestionPattern
Need to inject library/framework context?Tool Wrapper
Need consistent, template-based output?Generator
Need to score against a checklist?Reviewer
Need to gather requirements first?Inversion
Need strict multi-step workflow?Pipeline

Start with the question your task asks. If it spans multiple questions, compose the patterns.

Patterns Compose

Section titled “Patterns Compose”

These patterns are not mutually exclusive.

A Pipeline skill can include a Reviewer step at the end to double-check its own work. A Generator can rely on Inversion at the beginning to gather the necessary variables before filling its template. Thanks to ADK’s SkillToolset and progressive disclosure, your agent only spends context tokens on the exact patterns it needs at runtime.

This is the architectural advantage: instead of cramming complex, fragile instructions into a single system prompt, you decompose the behavior into composable building blocks. Each block is testable independently. Each block has a clear contract.

Practical Tips

Section titled “Practical Tips”

  1. Start with one pattern. Most tasks fit a single pattern cleanly. Don’t compose until you need to.

  2. Name the pattern in metadata. Adding metadata.pattern: tool-wrapper to your frontmatter makes the architecture explicit and searchable across your skill library.

  3. Keep references external. The power of Wrapper, Reviewer, and Pipeline patterns comes from loading context files on demand. Don’t inline large checklists or conventions into SKILL.md itself.

  4. Gate aggressively in Pipelines. Every checkpoint you skip is a validation you lose. The explicit “DO NOT proceed until…” instruction is the Pipeline’s most important line.

  5. Test patterns in isolation. A Generator with a broken template is a Generator problem, not a skill problem. Debug the pattern layer, not the SKILL.md layer.

Get Started

Section titled “Get Started”

The Agent Skills specification is open-source and natively supported across Google ADK. You already know how to package the format. Now you know how to design the content.

Stop formatting. Start architecting.

PM Skills Marketplace: 65 Agentic Skills That Turn Claude Code Into a Product Management Operating System

Mar 5, 2026
Vibe Sparking

PM Skills Marketplace: 65 Agentic Skills That Turn Claude Code Into a Product Management Operating System

Section titled “PM Skills Marketplace: 65 Agentic Skills That Turn Claude Code Into a Product Management Operating System”

You ask Claude to write a PRD. You get two pages of professional-sounding text that would embarrass anyone who’s actually read Inspired. The structure looks right, the words are in the right order, but there’s no Opportunity Solution Tree behind the feature list, no assumption mapping behind the priorities, no JTBD framing behind the user stories.

You know the frameworks. You’ve read Teresa Torres on continuous discovery, Marty Cagan on empowered product teams, Alberto Savoia on pretotyping, Dan Olsen on lean product. The problem isn’t knowledge. It’s that these frameworks sit on your bookshelf while Claude generates flat text at the speed of light.

Paweł Huryn — author of The Product Compass newsletter — built PM Skills Marketplace to close that gap.

What Is PM Skills Marketplace?

Section titled “What Is PM Skills Marketplace?”

65 skills. 36 chained workflows. 8 plugins. All open source, MIT licensed.

Each skill encodes a proven PM framework — not as a prompt template, but as domain knowledge that Claude draws on during conversation. When you discuss product discovery, Claude automatically loads Teresa Torres’s Opportunity Solution Tree methodology. When you prioritize features, it applies Impact × Risk matrices with experiment suggestions. When you test assumptions, it uses Alberto Savoia’s pretotyping approach from The Right It.

GitHub: phuryn/pm-skills Author: Paweł Huryn (The Product Compass) License: MIT Compatibility: Claude Code, Cowork, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Codex CLI, Kiro

Three-Layer Architecture

Section titled “Three-Layer Architecture”

The design is clean. Skills are building blocks. Commands chain skills into workflows. Plugins group everything by PM domain.

Skills

Section titled “Skills”

Each skill gives Claude domain knowledge for a specific PM task. Some are standalone references — prioritization-frameworks covers 9 frameworks (Opportunity Score, ICE, RICE, MoSCoW, Kano, etc.) that Claude draws on whenever you discuss prioritization. Others are workflow components that multiple commands share.

Skills load automatically when relevant to the conversation. No explicit invocation needed. If you want to force a specific one, use /plugin-name:skill-name.

Commands

Section titled “Commands”

Commands are where it gets interesting. /discover chains four skills together:

  1. brainstorm-ideas — multi-perspective ideation (PM, Designer, Engineer)
  2. identify-assumptions — risky assumptions across Value, Usability, Viability, Feasibility
  3. prioritize-assumptions — Impact × Risk matrix with experiment suggestions
  4. brainstorm-experiments — design lean experiments to test top assumptions

One command, full discovery cycle. And when it finishes, it suggests the next relevant command — just follow the prompts.

Plugins

Section titled “Plugins”

Eight plugins cover the PM lifecycle end to end:

PluginSkillsCommandsWhat It Covers
pm-product-discovery135Ideation, experiments, assumption testing, OST, interviews
pm-product-strategy125Strategy canvas, vision, business models, pricing, SWOT
pm-execution1510PRDs, OKRs, roadmaps, sprints, retros, user stories
pm-market-research73Personas, journey maps, market sizing, competitor analysis
pm-data-analytics33SQL generation, cohort analysis, A/B test analysis
pm-go-to-market63GTM strategy, beachhead segments, ICP, growth loops
pm-marketing-growth52Positioning, value props, product naming, North Star
pm-toolkit45Resume review, NDAs, privacy policies, proofreading

Installation

Section titled “Installation”

For Claude Code (Cowork):

  1. Open Customize (bottom-left)
  2. Go to Browse plugins → Personal → +
  3. Select Add marketplace from GitHub
  4. Enter: phuryn/pm-skills

All 8 plugins install automatically.

For Claude Code CLI:

For other tools (Gemini CLI, Cursor, Codex CLI, Kiro):

Skills work in any tool that reads SKILL.md files. Commands are Claude-specific.

Practical Workflows

Section titled “Practical Workflows”

Here’s where PM Skills differs from prompting. Instead of crafting elaborate prompts for each PM task, you get structured workflows that chain together.

New Product Idea? Start with /discover

Section titled “New Product Idea? Start with /discover”

This walks you through a complete discovery cycle. Ideation across three perspectives. Assumption identification across four risk categories. Prioritization using Impact × Risk. Experiment design using lean startup methods.

Need Strategic Clarity? Use /strategy

Section titled “Need Strategic Clarity? Use /strategy”

Builds a comprehensive 9-section Product Strategy Canvas: vision, target customer, value proposition, competitive advantage, growth strategy, revenue model, metrics, risks, and strategic bets.

Writing a PRD? Try /write-prd

Section titled “Writing a PRD? Try /write-prd”

Creates a comprehensive 8-section PRD — not generic boilerplate, but a structured document with the rigor of frameworks from Dan Olsen and Marty Cagan.

Preparing for Launch? Run /plan-launch

Section titled “Preparing for Launch? Run /plan-launch”

Full GTM strategy from beachhead segment identification through ICP definition, messaging, channels, and launch plan.

Defining Success? Set /north-star

Section titled “Defining Success? Set /north-star”

Defines your North Star Metric and supporting input metrics with business game classification.

The Intellectual Heritage

Section titled “The Intellectual Heritage”

What makes PM Skills valuable isn’t the tooling — it’s what’s encoded inside. The skills are built on work from:

  • Teresa Torres — Continuous Discovery Habits (Opportunity Solution Trees, assumption mapping)
  • Marty Cagan — INSPIRED and TRANSFORMED (empowered product teams, product strategy)
  • Alberto Savoia — The Right It (pretotyping, lean experiments)
  • Dan Olsen — The Lean Product Playbook (product-market fit methodology)
  • Roger L. Martin — Playing to Win (strategy choices)
  • Ash Maurya — Running Lean (Lean Canvas)
  • Strategyzer — Business Model Generation and Value Proposition Design
  • Christina Wodtke — Radical Focus (OKRs)
  • Anthony W. Ulwick — Jobs to Be Done
  • Alistair Croll & Benjamin Yoskovitz — Lean Analytics
  • Sean Ellis — Hacking Growth
  • Maja Voje — Go-To-Market Strategist

These aren’t name-drops. Each framework is embedded in the skill’s domain knowledge and guides Claude’s output structure.

What Makes This Different from Prompting?

Section titled “What Makes This Different from Prompting?”

Three things.

Structure, not templates. Skills give Claude domain knowledge, not fill-in-the-blank templates. The output adapts to your specific context while maintaining framework rigor.

Chained workflows. Commands link skills into sequences that mirror how PM work actually flows. Discovery feeds into strategy feeds into execution. You don’t manually orchestrate the pipeline.

Automatic loading. Skills activate when relevant to the conversation. Discuss pricing and Claude draws on pricing strategy, willingness-to-pay analysis, and competitive pricing models without you asking.

Who Is This For?

Section titled “Who Is This For?”

PMs who already know the frameworks and want them applied consistently. Founders doing PM work alongside engineering. Tech leads making product decisions without a dedicated PM. Anyone who’s read the books and wants the rigor without the overhead.

If you’ve never read Torres or Cagan, start with the books. PM Skills encodes expertise — it doesn’t replace understanding.

Rough Edges

Section titled “Rough Edges”

The commands (slash-command workflows) only work in Claude Code and Cowork. Other tools get the skills but not the chaining. The CSV-based story framework format is functional but not elegant. And like any AI tool, the output quality depends on the quality of your input — garbage context in, structured garbage out.

How to Build Your Content Knowledge System with AI: From Bookmark Hoarding to Knowledge Flow

Jan 21, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Introduction

Section titled “Introduction”

How many tweets are sitting in your bookmarks?

500? 1,000? Or are you afraid to even look?

You scroll past great content, hit bookmark, and think “I’ll organize this properly later.” And then? Nothing happens.

Those bookmarks are like books you bought but never opened, a gym membership you never used—their only purpose is to give you the illusion that “I’m learning.”

But actually, my friend, this is just a facade.

To put it bluntly: bookmarking never produces knowledge—execution does.

But here’s the good news: The AI era has given us a brand new opportunity.

In the past, knowledge management relied on willpower and time. Now, AI can become your “knowledge assistant”—helping you filter, categorize, organize, and even spark output.

This isn’t about using AI to replace thinking. It’s about using AI to unleash thinking.

The Trap I Fell Into

Section titled “The Trap I Fell Into”

I used to be a “bookmarking addict” too.

One day when I wanted to find a tweet about “pricing strategy,” I searched for 20 minutes and couldn’t find it. In that moment, I realized:

  1. I didn’t actually have mastery over the content I bookmarked
  2. This isn’t a knowledge base—it’s a garbage dump.

I spent three months rebuilding my content knowledge system. And the introduction of AI tools made this process 10x faster.

What’s the difference?

It’s not the tool—it’s the system. And AI is the engine that makes the system run automatically.

Core Understanding: Knowledge Management is a Loop

Section titled “Core Understanding: Knowledge Management is a Loop”

Most people’s knowledge management looks like this:

See good content → Bookmark → Forget → See good content → Bookmark → Forget…

This is a straight line, and it’s a dead end.

Truly effective knowledge management is a loop:

Acquire → Process → Organize → Output → Feed back into acquisition

Every step has clear actions, each serving the next. It’s not hoarding—it’s flow.

Let me break down my practical approach. No theory, just what I actually do every day.

Step 1: Information Acquisition—Not Everything Is Worth Saving

Section titled “Step 1: Information Acquisition—Not Everything Is Worth Saving”

First, ask yourself: What’s your standard for bookmarking a tweet?

If the answer is “feels useful,” you’re done for. “Feels useful” is the most useless standard.

My filtering criteria are only three:

  1. Can directly solve a clear problem or need I have (e.g., I’m researching pricing and see a pricing case study)
  2. Can become material for my future content (a counterintuitive insight, real data, a good story)
  3. Can change my cognitive framework (not information increment, but thinking method upgrade)

Anything that doesn’t meet these three doesn’t get bookmarked.

Yes, you read that right. Most “good content” isn’t worth saving because:

  • Universal wisdom—you’ll encounter it again eventually
  • Knowledge without context—you won’t use it even if saved
  • Things that make you “wow” but you can’t explain why—usually emotional value, not knowledge value

Bookmarking less is the first step of knowledge management.

For example, last week I scrolled past a tweet about “why free products are harder to sell.” Novel perspective, but I asked myself: Am I researching this? Can it be article material? Both answers were no. So I didn’t save it—just liked it and moved on.

Self-control is a skill.

AI Acceleration: Smart Filtering

Section titled “AI Acceleration: Smart Filtering”

How can AI help at this step? Quickly assess content value.

Now I use ChatGPT or Claude to assist with filtering. When I’m hesitant about whether content is worth saving, I throw it to AI and ask:

“What’s the core insight of this content? What problem does it solve? What scenario is it suitable for?”

AI gives me a structured answer in 10 seconds. If the answer makes me think “this is actually useful,” I save it. If the answer is vague, it means the content itself lacks practical value—I move on.

AI isn’t replacing your thinking—it’s helping you validate quickly.

Step 2: Information Processing—Making Bookmarks “Searchable”

Section titled “Step 2: Information Processing—Making Bookmarks “Searchable””

OK, let’s say you’ve learned restraint and your bookmarks only contain truly valuable content. What’s next?

Categorization.

But not that silly “learning/work/life” classification. Three months later, even you won’t know why you categorized it that way.

My classification logic is purpose-based:

  • Material Library: Cases, data, quotable lines you can directly reference
  • Methodologies: Reusable frameworks, processes, checklists by type
  • Inspiration Pool: Perspectives that triggered thinking, but I’m not sure how to use yet
  • Pending: Topics needing deep research when I have time

Every time I save a bookmark, I spend 5 seconds doing one thing: choosing which folder it lives in.

For example:

  • Original tweet: “Users won’t pay for products, they only pay for solutions”
  • My classification: “Pricing—Value Anchoring”

Those 5 seconds determine whether you can find it three months from now.

A bookmark without notes is a house without an address. You know it exists, but you’ll never find it.

AI Acceleration: Auto-Classification + Tag Generation

Section titled “AI Acceleration: Auto-Classification + Tag Generation”

This is where AI shines brightest.

I batch send a group of bookmarks (say, 10 items) to AI and have it help me:

  1. Auto-categorize: Based on my classification system, suggest which folder each item belongs in
  2. Generate tags: Create 2-3 keyword tags for each item
  3. Extract summaries: Summarize the core insight in one sentence

My prompt template:

What used to take 1 hour to organize 10 items now takes 5 minutes.

AI automates the mechanical labor—you just need to do the final confirmation.

Step 3: Knowledge Organization—From Fragments to System

Section titled “Step 3: Knowledge Organization—From Fragments to System”

Bookmarks are just a transit station, not the destination.

Every Sunday night I spend 1 hour doing one thing: emptying my bookmarks.

Not deleting—transferring. Moving bookmarked content into Feishu (Lark) documents.

My Feishu document structure is simple:

When transferring each piece of content, I do three things:

  1. Extract core insight: Summarize in one sentence, under 20 characters
  2. Mark source: Who said it, when, original link
  3. Write my thinking: Do I agree or disagree? Why? What can it connect to?

The third point is most important. Organization without thinking is just hoarding in a different place.

AI Acceleration: Deep Organization + Connection Discovery

Section titled “AI Acceleration: Deep Organization + Connection Discovery”

AI can do two things at this step:

First, help you do deep organization.

When you throw a piece of content to AI, you can ask:

“What’s the underlying logic of this perspective? What are the prerequisites? What are the limitations?”

AI helps you break down a fragmented piece of content into structured knowledge. This is 10x faster than thinking it through yourself, and often reveals angles you hadn’t noticed.

Second, help you discover connections.

I periodically batch-send content from my knowledge base to AI and ask:

“What connections exist between these items? Can they be combined into a new perspective or article framework?”

AI helps you do “knowledge connecting”—this is exactly the core capability of a Second Brain.

I’ve found that many viral article ideas emerge from this “AI helps you connect” process.

Here’s a real example.

Three months ago I bookmarked a tweet that said “don’t chase 10,000 followers, chase 100 true fans.” My note was “Personal Brand—Follower Quality.”

During Sunday organization, I put it in the “Personal Brand” folder and wrote:

“I agree with half of this. 100 true fans are indeed more valuable than 10,000 passersby, but the premise is you know how to find those 100 people and how to serve them. Most people’s problem isn’t ‘chasing quantity’—it’s ‘they don’t even have quantity.’ This can be written in contrast to the ‘1,000 True Fans’ article.”

Two weeks later, I wrote “Don’t Be Fooled by ‘100 True Fans’“—readership was 3x my usual.

Materials don’t become content on their own—thinking does.

Why Most People’s Knowledge Management Fails

Section titled “Why Most People’s Knowledge Management Fails”

Now that we’ve covered methods, let’s talk mindset.

I’ve observed many people’s knowledge management. Failure usually comes down to three reasons:

1. Treating Collection as Learning

Section titled “1. Treating Collection as Learning”

The moment you bookmark, your brain releases dopamine, giving you the illusion that “I learned something.” But actually, you just moved someone else’s knowledge from their brain to your hard drive.

Knowledge only truly belongs to you after it passes through your thinking, your practice, your output.

2. System Too Complex, Can’t Persist

Section titled “2. System Too Complex, Can’t Persist”

I’ve seen people build super complex knowledge bases in Notion—50+ tags alone, plus all kinds of relationships and views. The day they finished building, they posted on WeChat Moments, then never opened it again.

The best system is the one you’re willing to use every day.

Simple enough to require no willpower—that’s how you sustain.

3. Input Only, No Output

Section titled “3. Input Only, No Output”

What’s the ultimate purpose of knowledge management? Not to make you a “mobile library,” but to enable you to use this knowledge.

Writing articles, giving presentations, solving problems, helping others—these are knowledge exits. A knowledge base without exits is a dead pool.

My rule for myself: for every 10 pieces of content organized, I must output 1 piece.

It can be a tweet, an article, or a share with a friend.

Output drives input—only then can this loop spin.

AI Acceleration: Content Generation + Perspective Assistance

Section titled “AI Acceleration: Content Generation + Perspective Assistance”

Many people know they should output, but get stuck on “don’t know what to write” or “can’t write it out.” AI can solve this problem.

My writing workflow:

  1. Let AI help you find topics: Send your recent knowledge notes to AI and ask “What articles could these become? Suggest 3 topics and angles”
  2. Let AI help you outline: Once you pick a topic, ask “What angles should I write about this? Give me an article framework”
  3. Let AI help you expand perspectives: After writing a section, ask “How can I make this point deeper? What counterexamples or supplementary views exist?”

Note: AI is a writing assistant, not a writing replacement. Your perspectives, your stories, your writing style—AI can’t replace these. But AI can help you convert knowledge into content faster.

4 Actions You Can Start Today

Section titled “4 Actions You Can Start Today”

With all that said, here are four things you can do today:

Action 1: Clean Your Bookmarks

Section titled “Action 1: Clean Your Bookmarks”

Open your Twitter bookmarks, delete everything that “feels useful but you can’t say why.” Target: cut 50%.

Be ruthless. Things you won’t use—keeping them only increases anxiety.

Action 2: Build Your Classification System

Section titled “Action 2: Build Your Classification System”

No need for complexity—four folders are enough: Materials, Methods, Inspiration, Pending.

Starting today, every time you save, put it in the corresponding folder and add a one-sentence note.

Action 3: Set an “Empty Day”

Section titled “Action 3: Set an “Empty Day””

Pick a fixed time each week to transfer bookmarks into your knowledge base. 30 minutes is enough.

Key isn’t duration—it’s regularity. Only fixed creates habits, habits create sustainability.

Action 4: Pick One AI Tool and Start Using It

Section titled “Action 4: Pick One AI Tool and Start Using It”

You don’t need to use every AI tool—just pick one:

  • ChatGPT or Claude: For content filtering, classification tagging, deep organization
  • Notion AI or Lark AI: For smart summaries and connections within documents
  • Readwise + Reader: For automatic syncing and annotation management

Start using it first, then optimize. Don’t fall into the “finding the best tool” trap.

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

Knowledge management has no magic tools, no perfect methodology.

Core is one sentence: Let knowledge flow.

Acquire, Process, Organize, Output, repeat.

With AI joining in, this loop spins faster and with less effort. But remember: AI is an accelerator, not a replacement. The ability to think, to judge, to express—these will always be yours.

Your knowledge base doesn’t need to be huge—it just needs to be alive.

Reference Links

Section titled “Reference Links”
  • Original Twitter Thread: @yaohui12138
  • Related Reading: “1,000 True Fans” by Kevin Kelly
  • AI Tools: ChatGPT | Claude | Notion AI
  • Knowledge Management Tools: Readwise | Lark/Feishu | Obsidian

  • Knowledge Management

  • Second Brain
  • Content Creation

Multi-Agent Systems for Beginners: Boost Your Claude Code Efficiency by 90%

Jan 20, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Multi-Agent Systems for Beginners: Boost Your Claude Code Efficiency by 90%

Section titled “Multi-Agent Systems for Beginners: Boost Your Claude Code Efficiency by 90%”

A comprehensive guide to building your first Multi-Agent system in Claude Code—no PhD required. Whether you’re a programmer or not, this guide will take you from curious beginner to confident AI team conductor.

Source: @0xYuker

Introduction: Why Multi-Agent Matters

Section titled “Introduction: Why Multi-Agent Matters”

The challenge in building powerful AI applications isn’t making a single agent smarter—it’s about orchestrating multiple agents effectively. Single agents hit ceilings quickly: context windows overflow, specialization suffers, and serial processing bottlenecks appear.

Multi-agent systems solve this by breaking complex tasks into specialized components, much like assembling a team of experts rather than relying on one generalist.

The Evidence from Anthropic

Section titled “The Evidence from Anthropic”

According to internal evaluation data from Claude Code’s creator Anthropic:

A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as “lead” and multiple Claude Sonnet 4 as “workers” performed 90.2% better on research tasks than a single strongest Claude Opus 4 agent.

This demonstrates that “team power” applies equally in the AI world, delivering:

  • Specialization: Higher expertise levels per domain
  • Parallel Processing: Shorter project cycles
  • Maintainability: Quick problem isolation
  • Scalability: Add new capabilities by adding new agents

The trade-off? Coordination overhead. Agents need to communicate, share information, and avoid stepping on each other’s toes. Understanding the right “team management” approach—orchestration patterns—is critical!

Part 1: Three Core Team Management Patterns

Section titled “Part 1: Three Core Team Management Patterns”

After industry validation, three mainstream multi-agent orchestration patterns emerge. Choose based on your task’s coordination needs, not which sounds coolest!

1. Supervisor Pattern (Centralized Control)

Section titled “1. Supervisor Pattern (Centralized Control)”

The most intuitive and common pattern. Imagine a project manager coordinating all work: one “supervisor” agent receives tasks, decomposes them into subtasks, assigns them to different “worker” agents, then supervises, verifies, and integrates all results.

Workflow: User request → Manager decomposes → Assigns to Sub-Agents → Agents execute → Manager validates + synthesizes → Final output

Pros/Cons: Clear control flow, easy to debug and audit. But supervisor becomes a bottleneck—all coordination is serial, increasing latency and token costs.

Claude Code Example:

2. Pipeline Pattern (Sequential)

Section titled “2. Pipeline Pattern (Sequential)”

Here, Sub-Agents execute in a fixed sequence—each agent’s output becomes the next agent’s input.

Workflow: Like an assembly line factory—latter input equals former output

Pros/Cons: Extremely stable, easy to debug. But equally fragile—if one stage jams, the whole line collapses.

Claude Code Example:

3. Concurrent Pattern (Map-Reduce)

Section titled “3. Concurrent Pattern (Map-Reduce)”

This pattern is essentially opening multiple Claude Code windows simultaneously and assigning them different tasks.

Workflow: Claude Code decomposes requirements and assigns to different agents

Pros/Cons: GBs of documents that might take one agent hours can be processed by multiple agents in minutes. But tasks must be “decomposable.”

Claude Code Example:

Part 2: Building a Four-Agent System

Section titled “Part 2: Building a Four-Agent System”

Creating individual specialists is step one. The real power is making them collaborate. Let’s build a community-popular Four-Agent workflow in Claude Code.

Four-Agent System Overview

Section titled “Four-Agent System Overview”

This system includes four roles, each with clear responsibilities:

They communicate through a shared Markdown file MULTI_AGENT_PLAN.md—a perfect example of “shared state” communication strategy.

Step 1: Create 4 Sub-Agents

Section titled “Step 1: Create 4 Sub-Agents”

If you don’t know how, see Manus Alternative: Claude Code Sub-Agent Beginner Guide.

You can generate them via Claude Code. Quick start—copy these prompts:

You should end up with four Sub-Agents:

Step 2: Initialize Project and Plan

Section titled “Step 2: Initialize Project and Plan”

In a new project folder, start Claude Code and issue your first command to the “architect”:

Use the architect agent. Our task is to build a user authentication system supporting registration, login, and password reset. Research best practices, then create a MULTI_AGENT_PLAN.md file and decompose initial tasks.

If successful, you’ll see the Architect Sub-Agent working:

Once complete, a clear task document (MULTI_AGENT_PLAN) appears with a work summary:

Step 3: Execute and Collaborate!

Section titled “Step 3: Execute and Collaborate!”

Now you can command multiple agents simultaneously. The simplest approach in one session:

Use the builder agent, start executing task 1 from MULTI_AGENT_PLAN.md

If you see the Builder Agent working and executing steps from the plan—congratulations! 🎉 Go grab a coffee and let it work.

The Builder agent will complete subtasks according to the architect’s assignment:

For parallelizable tasks, it may even launch multiple Sub-Agents simultaneously:

Mind-blowing, right? 🤯

After Builder completes, Claude Code calls remaining Sub-Agents for testing and documentation:

A Real Success Story

Section titled “A Real Success Story”

A Reddit user shared their experience building a “Supplement-Drug Interaction Checker”:

By letting four specialized AI programs collaborate like a professional team, you can dramatically improve work efficiency!

Conclusion: Become an AI Team Commander Today

Section titled “Conclusion: Become an AI Team Commander Today”

We’ve covered a journey—from understanding why multi-agent matters, to mastering core orchestration patterns, to building and commanding your first AI agent team in Claude Code. You’ve likely discovered this is more than a technical innovation—it’s a complete paradigm shift in how we work.

Two final pieces of advice:

First, start with the simplest pattern. Don’t try building a ten-agent complex system on day one. Start with one Sub-Agent, observe where it struggles, add a second to solve that problem, then add a supervisor. Iterate, iterate, iterate.

Second, you’re the commander, not a spectator. AI Agents are powerful tools, but they need your guidance and decisions. Learn to give clear commands, correct errors promptly, and provide the context and tools agents need. The depth of your collaboration with your AI team will determine your ultimate success.

Now, pick up the baton and go create your future.

Recommended Scenarios & Best Practices

When to Use It

Section titled “When to Use It”
ScenarioPain PointDesign and Refine Solution
Starting new component/pageUncertain direction, afraid of wrong choiceGenerate exploratory variations, compare
Redesigning existing UIWant to see alternativesGenerate alternatives, discover new approaches
Stuck on design directionNot sure what you wantLet AI provide options, break mental blocks
Getting stakeholder buy-inVerbal descriptions fall flatShow concrete variations, visually compelling
Learning what worksWant to understand layouts/densitiesExperience differences in your actual codebase

Usage Workflow

Section titled “Usage Workflow”

Start a session:

What happens next:

  1. Preflight — Detects your framework (Next.js, Vite, etc.) and styling system (Tailwind, MUI, etc.)

  2. Style inference — Reads your existing design tokens from Tailwind config, CSS variables, or theme files

  3. Interview — AI asks about:

    • What you’re designing (component vs page, new vs redesign)
    • Pain points and what should improve
    • Visual and interaction inspiration
    • Target user and key tasks

  4. Generation — Creates 5 distinct variations exploring different:

    • Information hierarchy
    • Layout models (cards, lists, tables, split-pane)
    • Density (compact vs spacious)
    • Interaction patterns (modal, inline, drawer)
    • Visual expression

  5. Review — Open http://localhost:3000/__design_lab (or your dev server port) to see all variations side-by-side

  6. Feedback — Tell Claude:

    • If one is already good → select it, make minor tweaks
    • If you like parts of different ones → describe what you like about each, get a synthesized version

  7. Iterate — Repeat until you’re confident

  8. Finalize — All temp files are deleted, DESIGN_PLAN.md is generated with implementation steps

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”

Be specific in the interview. The more context you give about pain points, target users, and inspiration, the more distinct and useful the variations will be.

Reference products you admire. “Like Linear’s density” or “Stripe’s clarity” gives Claude concrete direction.

Don’t settle on round one. The synthesis step is where it gets good—describe what you like about each variant and let it combine them.

Keep your dev server running. The plugin won’t start it for you (that would block). Just have it running in another terminal.

Check the DESIGN_PLAN.md. After finalizing, this file contains the implementation steps, component API, accessibility checklist, and testing guidance.

A: Yes, Design and Refine is a Claude Code plugin and requires Claude Code environment.

A: Yes, but recommend testing and tweaking based on actual requirements.

A: Yes! The plugin auto-infers design specs from Tailwind config, CSS variables, or theme files.

OpenContext: A Personal Context Store for AI Agents and Assistants

Introduction

Section titled “Introduction”

When working with AI assistants like Claude Code or Cursor, one persistent challenge emerges: context gets lost. Across different projects, days, or chat sessions, you find yourself re-explaining background, repeating design decisions, and sometimes the AI continues with wrong assumptions.

OpenContext solves this problem by providing a lightweight personal context/knowledge store that AI agents can read from and write to - giving your AI assistant a persistent memory.

The Problem OpenContext Solves

Section titled “The Problem OpenContext Solves”

📂 Hard to share context across repos/sessions✅ Global context library works across all projects
🤷 Your ideas can’t be quickly perceived by Agent✅ Agent loads your background & decisions automatically
🔒 Existing knowledge can’t be operated by Coding Agent✅ Agent can directly read/write your knowledge base

OpenContext provides a comprehensive toolkit for context management:

  • oc CLI — Manage a global contexts/ library (folders, docs, manifests, search)
  • MCP Server — Let Cursor/Agents call OpenContext as tools
  • Desktop App — Manage/search/edit contexts with native UI

A:

  • Project-level (.claude/skills/): Skills available only for that project
  • User-level (~/.claude/skills/): Skills available across all projects
  • Skill Manager itself should be installed at the user level for maximum utility

CodMate: The Ultimate macOS Session Manager for CLI AI Tools

Vibe Sparking

Introduction

Section titled “Introduction”

If you’re a developer who uses CLI-based AI tools like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI, you know the pain of managing hundreds of scattered session files. Finding that brilliant solution from last Tuesday, resuming a suspended project context, or even just reviewing what you accomplished can be frustrating.

Enter CodMate—a native macOS SwiftUI application that brings order to your AI coding chaos. Built with performance in mind and designed for developers who value their time, CodMate transforms how you interact with your AI programming assistants.

What is CodMate?

Section titled “What is CodMate?”

CodMate is a session manager for CLI AI tools that provides:

  • Multi-source session browsing supporting Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI
  • Blazing-fast search with incremental indexing and caching
  • Compact three-column UI designed for efficient workflow
  • “Ship it” workflows like Project Review with Git Changes
  • One-click Resume/New functionality

Built with Swift 6 and SwiftUI, CodMate leverages macOS 13.5+ APIs to deliver a truly native experience with universal binary support (Apple Silicon + Intel).

Key Features

Section titled “Key Features”

Lightning-Fast Search & Navigation

Section titled “Lightning-Fast Search & Navigation”

CodMate’s global search panel (⌘F) offers scoped search with progress/cancel capabilities, plus quick list filtering. The app uses:

  • Memory-mapped reads for fast path indexing
  • Incremental parsing (first ~64 lines + tail sampling)
  • Background enrichment with constrained task groups
  • Chunked full-text search (128 KB) that avoids loading entire files

Project & Task Organization

Section titled “Project & Task Organization”

Keep your work organized with:

  • Projects that group sessions by repository
  • Tasks that group sessions by goal
  • Shareable task context files for team collaboration
  • Auto-assignment for new sessions in active projects

Section titled “Terminal Integration”

Resume sessions directly into your preferred terminal:

  • Terminal.app
  • iTerm2
  • Warp
  • Embedded terminal (non-sandbox builds)

Project Review (Git Changes)

Section titled “Project Review (Git Changes)”

One of CodMate’s most powerful features is the Project Review mode, which shows:

  • Changed files with stage/unstage support
  • Unified diff or raw preview
  • Commit UI with AI-powered commit message generation
  • On-demand repo authorization

MCP Server Management

Section titled “MCP Server Management”

CodMate includes comprehensive MCP server support:

  • Uni-Import (paste/drag JSON configuration)
  • Per-server enable toggles
  • Per-target toggles (Codex/Claude/Gemini)

  • Automatic export to ~/.claude/settings.json

FAQ

Q: Does CodMate modify my session files?

A: No, CodMate only reads session files. Notes, project assignments, and other metadata are stored separately.

Q: Can I use CodMate with multiple CLI tools simultaneously?

A: Yes! CodMate supports Codex, Claude Code, and Gemini CLI concurrently.

Q: Is my session data sent anywhere?

A: CodMate is local-first. Your session data never leaves your Mac unless you explicitly use features that call external APIs (like AI commit message generation).

Liquid AI Cookbook: Examples, Tutorials and Apps Built with LFM Models

Jan 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Introduction

Section titled “Introduction”

As artificial intelligence continues to evolve, the demand for efficient, deployable models that can run on edge devices has grown significantly. Liquid AI has emerged as a key player in this space with their open-weight LFM (Liquid Foundation Models) and the open-source LEAP SDK.

The Liquid AI Cookbook is a comprehensive repository containing examples, tutorials, and applications built with these technologies. Whether you’re looking to customize models, deploy to laptops and edge devices, or build complete applications, this cookbook provides the resources to get started.

What is Liquid AI?

Section titled “What is Liquid AI?”

Liquid AI is developing a new generation of hybrid models designed specifically for on-device deployment. Their LFM2 models range from 350M to 8B parameters, making them ideal for edge deployment while maintaining strong performance on agentic tasks, data extraction, RAG, creative writing, and multi-turn conversations.

Key Characteristics

Section titled “Key Characteristics”
  • Hybrid Architecture: Combines different modeling techniques for efficiency
  • On-Device First: Designed from the ground up for edge deployment
  • Specialized Models: Task-specific checkpoints for extraction, RAG, tool use, and math
  • Multi-Modal Support: Vision-language models (LFM2-VL) for visual understanding
  • Edge SDK: Native framework for mobile deployment (Android/iOS)

LFM2 Model Family

Section titled “LFM2 Model Family”

Text-to-Text Models

Section titled “Text-to-Text Models”

The LFM2 series is designed for agentic tasks and on-device deployment:

ModelSizeBest For
LFM2-8B-A1B8BComplex reasoning, multi-turn conversations
LFM2-2.6B2.6BBalanced performance and efficiency
LFM2-1.2B1.2BMobile deployment, real-time applications
LFM2-700M700MResource-constrained environments
LFM2-350M350MUltra-low latency scenarios

Specialized Nano Models

Section titled “Specialized Nano Models”

For specific use cases, Liquid AI offers specialized “nano” checkpoints:

ModelUse Cases
LFM2-1.2B-ExtractData extraction from unstructured text (emails, filings, tickets)
LFM2-1.2B-RAGRAG applications, chatbots, knowledge base Q&A
LFM2-1.2B-ToolReal-time API calls, database queries, system integrations
LFM2-350M-MathMathematical problem solving and reasoning

Vision-Language Models

Section titled “Vision-Language Models”
ModelSizeDescription
LFM2-VL-1.6B1.6BGeneral vision-language tasks
LFM2-VL-450M450MLightweight visual understanding

Example Applications

Section titled “Example Applications”

The cookbook includes several ready-to-run examples:

Invoice Parser

Section titled “Invoice Parser”

A Python CLI that extracts structured data from invoice images using a 2-step agentic workflow. Perfect for automating document processing tasks.

Audio Transcription CLI

Section titled “Audio Transcription CLI”

Real-time audio-to-text transcription using LFM2-Audio-1.5B with llama.cpp integration. Ideal for meeting notes, podcast transcripts, and voice memos.

LEAP Edge SDK

Section titled “LEAP Edge SDK”

The LEAP Edge SDK is Liquid AI’s native framework for running LFM2 models on mobile devices. It provides:

  • Native Support: Android (Kotlin) and iOS (Swift)
  • Simple API: As easy as calling cloud LLM endpoints
  • Real-Time Streaming: Token streaming for responsive chat experiences
  • Persistent History: Built-in conversation management

Android Examples

Alma comes from yetone, the same developer behind OpenAI Translator — a wildly popular project with 23.1k+ GitHub stars. That project evolved from a Chrome extension into a multi-platform desktop app, demonstrating yetone’s ability to build polished, production-ready tools.

Web Search Integration
